faqs.q: Which AI development service do I need?
faqs.a: Start from the problem. If people need answers from your documents, choose the chatbot service. To pull data out of PDFs, choose document AI. For apps and APIs choose Python backend. faqs.q: Do I need clean, labelled data before an AI project can start?
faqs.a: No. Looking at what you have is part of the first step. I check a small sample of your documents, recordings, images or tables and tell you early what is usable, what needs cleaning and whether you need more examples. Labelled data matters most for the machine learning work.

faqs.q: Is my idea suited to AI, or would simple software do?

faqs.q: What is a RAG chatbot?
faqs.a: A RAG chatbot looks up the right passages in your own documents first and only then writes its answer from them. RAG stands for retrieval-augmented generation. Because the answer is built from your documents, it can show its source. It can also say "not found" when the documents do not cover the question, instead of guessing.

faqs.q: How do you stop a chatbot from making things up?
faqs.a: With several layers, not one instruction. First the chatbot checks that the documents really contain the answer. Weak matches never reach the AI language model (LLM), the part that writes the reply. A fixed fallback sentence covers the rest. In my healthcare example, out-of-scope questions get a plain "not found" instead of a guess.

faqs.q: Can a chatbot run on my own servers?
faqs.a: Often, yes. At work I build on AI models hosted on the client's own servers, so no data or prompts leave the building. My personal projects use online services such as Groq. During planning we choose what fits your privacy needs, budget and answer quality.

faqs.q: How much does an AI chatbot cost for a website?
faqs.a: I do not publish a price list, because chatbots vary a lot. The cost depends on how many documents you have, how they are organised, where the chatbot must run and how much testing you need. After reading your brief I suggest a fixed price or hourly billing. We agree it in writing before I start.

faqs.q: What kinds of documents can the chatbot use?
faqs.a: Text-based documents such as policies, manuals, circulars and support articles. Tables and images inside documents can be harder, so we test those early. I start with a small sample of yours to check how well the chatbot finds the right passages, before we commit to the full build.

faqs.q: Can my team maintain it after you finish?
faqs.a: That is the aim. Instructions and adjustable settings live in simple settings files, and the code has tests. The handover includes a walkthrough of how to add documents and tune the settings. If you want ongoing help, we can agree a maintenance period in writing.

faqs.q: What happens when our documents change?
faqs.a: The search index is rebuilt from the updated files. In my healthcare example, an ingest step can wipe and rebuild the index, and identical passages are not stored twice. It does not yet watch for file changes or keep old versions apart. For a client I would add both, so outdated wording cannot answer a new question.

faqs.q: Does the chatbot need training on our documents?
faqs.a: No training run is needed. When a question arrives, the chatbot searches your documents for the best passages, so updating it means changing the files and refreshing the search index, not retraining a model. In my language model projects, quality came from retrieval, checks and prompts, not from training a model.

problems.problem: The bot misreads what the user is asking for
problems.approach: I design flows around what the user wants. A simple router sends document questions, booking requests and small talk to different handlers, and chat history lives in a database. In client chatbot work this reduced failures during complex bookings.

problems.problem: A hosted AI model is retired or slows down
problems.approach: Model names and fallback order live in settings, so the service switches to a backup model without a code change, and each reply states which model answered. Request IDs plus metrics and traces, as built in my Traceable AI Backend, make a silent switch visible.

problems.problem: You cannot tell if a change made answers better or worse
problems.approach: I keep a list of questions with the expected answers, including ones the documents should not answer. My healthcare example has such a list, checked by hand; for a client I add automatic scoring on every change.

problems.problem: Visitors try to trick or flood the chatbot
problems.approach: On the scam honeypot I added a filter for prompt-injection attempts (messages that try to override the AI's instructions) and a request limit of 1 per second per visitor, with bursts of 5. For a client I would add a test set of attacks.

tradeoffs.title: Online AI service or your own servers
tradeoffs.text: Online services such as Groq or OpenAI are quick to start. Hosting the model on your own servers keeps every document and prompt in-house but needs a stronger machine. I usually prototype on non-sensitive samples, then decide with you.

tradeoffs.title: Strict answers or more answers
tradeoffs.text: A high match score gives more "not found" replies and fewer wrong answers. A low score answers more questions but risks mistakes. For policy, health or finance content I suggest starting strict and loosening only after testing real questions.

tradeoffs.title: Remember the conversation or not
tradeoffs.text: Memory lets a user ask a follow-up, but it needs stored history, privacy rules and more testing. My healthcare example answers each question on its own. For customer chat I store history in a database. I add memory only when the use case needs it.

faqs.q: What is document AI?
faqs.a: Document AI is software that reads documents such as PDFs, forms and reports. It turns what they say into structured data you can search, check and use. It can pull out names, dates, amounts and obligations. I build it so every extracted fact links back to the exact quote in the source document.

faqs.q: How much does document AI cost?
faqs.a: It depends on the number and variety of your documents, the accuracy you need and where the tool must run. I do not publish a price list. After a short brief and a test on a sample of your files, I suggest a fixed price or hourly billing. We agree it in writing before I start.

faqs.q: How accurate is AI data extraction from PDFs?
faqs.a: Accuracy is measured on your own files and reported plainly. I build a scoring tool that compares the output with a small set of correct answers from your documents, then fix the mistakes it finds. On a regulatory project, 97.2% of 1,266 production records link to an exact passage; that measures traceability, not completeness.

faqs.q: Can my documents stay on our own servers?
faqs.a: Yes, and that is a common requirement. Several systems I work on use AI models hosted on the client's own servers, so documents, prompts and usage records stay on the machine. During planning we check what hardware is available, because larger models need stronger machines.

faqs.q: How do you stop AI from adding invented details?
faqs.a: With checks in code, not just instructions in a prompt. In the audit drafting service I built, any figure, date or owner that is not in the source note causes the draft to be rejected automatically. In 27 checked draft versions, a small sample, I found no invented facts. A reviewer still accepts, edits or rejects every draft.

faqs.q: Can this connect to our existing product?
faqs.a: Yes. I connected an AI drafting service to a live product built with Spring Boot and React. It runs as a separate FastAPI service. There is a clear agreement about the data it sends and receives. The main product and the new service can be updated separately.

faqs.q: Will the AI find every item in a long document?
faqs.a: No. In a controlled comparison on documents held back from tuning, recall (how many of the real obligations were found) rose from 32% to 69% on Basel III rules and from 69% to 82% on KYC (know-your-customer) rules. Some are still missed, so every result links to its source and a person reviews the list.

faqs.q: Can it read scanned pages and invoices?
faqs.a: PDFs that already contain typed text are the easiest. Scanned pages and photos first need text recognition (OCR), and results depend on scan quality, so I test a sample of your scans before agreeing a plan. My case studies here cover regulatory PDFs, audit notes and a database, not invoices.

problems.approach: Code compares each draft with the source note and rejects it if it adds a figure, date or owner. On the audit drafting service, 0 invented facts were found across 27 checked draft versions.

problems.problem: Nobody knows how accurate the output really is
problems.approach: I build the scoring step first and run it on a sample of your documents. On the database project, simple scoring suggested about 93% quality, but running the queries showed a far lower true figure.

problems.approach: I build it as a separate FastAPI service with a clear data contract: an agreed shape for what it sends and receives. The audit service was connected to an existing Spring Boot and React product, and the client adopted it the day after handover.

tradeoffs.title: Find every item or only sure ones
tradeoffs.text: Tuning to catch every item raises recall (the share of items found) but adds wrong extras. Tuning for certainty raises precision (the share of found items that are correct) but misses items. I ask which mistake costs you more, then report both on your documents.

tradeoffs.title: Bigger AI model or faster answers
tradeoffs.text: A larger model may read more carefully but is slower and needs a stronger machine. I compare candidate models on your documents against a time limit you set, as I did with four models on the audit drafting service.

tradeoffs.title: Fully automatic or reviewed by a person
tradeoffs.text: For compliance and audit work I keep a person in charge. Each item links to its source, and a reviewer can accept, edit or reject it. Full automation only suits low-risk fields where accuracy has been measured.

faqs.q: Is FastAPI used in production?
faqs.a: Yes. Many companies use FastAPI in production for web services and AI features. It is fast, checks incoming data automatically and writes API documentation for you. faqs.q: How accurate is computer vision?

problems.approach: In project work I keep test footage apart from training footage, split by video, and state the split beside every figure. The team deepfake detector's 74.16% is labelled as a random frame-level split, because near-identical frames from one video can sit on both sides.

problems.approach: Simple background removal can undercount when people overlap. I test on your hardest footage and report where the tool fails. For crowded scenes I can switch to a trained detector with a tracker (it follows each person from frame to frame).

problems.approach: Each result keeps the evidence behind it. In the deepfake app, a chart scores every frame, a note explains each confidence band and a PDF report can be downloaded. The CCTV prototype saves its evidence frames in MongoDB.

problems.approach: Alerts go to a channel your staff already use. The CCTV prototype I worked on sent a WhatsApp message through Twilio when the crowd limit was reached, with a reference to the saved frame.

tradeoffs.text: A detector can be tuned to raise fewer false alarms or to miss fewer real events, but not both at once. We agree which mistake costs more for you, set the alert level to match and report both kinds of error.

faqs.a: A trained model is wrapped in a small FastAPI service with tests and a Docker setup, the same way I build other backends. Your apps can then send data to it and read the result. Handover includes instructions for running it, so your team can move it to a server or cloud machine later.

faqs.q: How much data do I need to train a model?
faqs.a: It depends on the task. Simple tasks with clear categories may need a few hundred labelled examples per category, while audio or images usually need thousands. My spam filter used 5,169 messages after duplicates were removed, and my speech model 12,162 clips. I count your examples first and tell you early if there are too few.

faqs.q: Can you classify my own audio or text data?
faqs.a: Yes, if you have labelled examples and a clear target. I have built a neural network on audio features. I have also built a spam classifier on text (word-frequency scoring with a Naive Bayes classifier). Each has a small app around it. Before training, we check that you have enough examples of each category.

faqs.q: How do you report accuracy?
faqs.a: Every figure comes with the data split it was measured on. The speech emotion model I retrained reaches 93.87% on a random 20% test split. Because that split can put altered copies of one clip on both sides, it says little about new voices. For your recordings I test on speakers the model has not heard.

faqs.q: Do you use ready-made models?
faqs.a: When they fit. Pretrained Hugging Face models are a sensible start for many text and audio tasks. My speech model began as a public training recipe that I retrained and tested on four datasets. I compare against a simple baseline, so you see what extra complexity buys, and I say when the simple option is enough.

faqs.q: Can you build a prediction model from my spreadsheet data?
faqs.a: Yes, if you have past rows with the outcome you want to predict, such as a price or cost. I clean the table, fill gaps, compare a simple linear baseline with a stronger model such as a Random Forest, and report the typical error in your own units. A small app lets your team try it.

faqs.q: How do you check a model has not just memorised its data?
faqs.a: I keep a test set the model never trains on and compare its score there with its training score. A large gap means it has memorised. The speech network I retrained also uses dropout (switching off random parts during training) to limit this. For your audio, altered copies of a clip stay on one side of the split.

faqs.q: Can you check the accuracy of a model someone else built?
faqs.a: Yes. I need the saved model or code, the data it used and the figure that was claimed. I rerun it, check how the data was split, compare it with a simple baseline and report what I measure. The same habit exposed a flattering 93% score on a bank text-to-SQL assistant, where running the queries showed far less.

who.need: Teams that want to flag tone or mood in recorded calls or check-ins, such as calls worth a follow-up, and need to know how far the labels can be trusted.

problems.problem: A model's accuracy figure cannot be trusted
problems.approach: In project work I hold back a test set the model never sees, split by speaker or source where possible, and state the split. I report precision (how many flags were right) and recall (how many real cases were found), not accuracy alone.

problems.problem: It is unclear whether a complex model is needed
problems.approach: I train a simple baseline first, then the stronger model, and report both. In my house-price model a Random Forest (many decision trees averaged) reached an R-squared of 0.89 (1.0 is perfect) against 0.80 for a simple linear baseline, both on held-out houses.

problems.problem: Raw audio and text are not ready for a model
problems.approach: Audio becomes numbers for loudness (energy), how often the signal crosses zero and MFCCs (a compact description of a voice's sound), extracted with librosa. Text is cleaned and scored by word frequency (TF-IDF). Tables get gaps filled and values scaled.

problems.problem: Too few labelled examples
problems.approach: Before any training I count examples per category and report gaps early. Where audio is scarce, altering clips with noise and pitch changes adds variety: in the speech model I retrained, 12,162 clips became 48,648 samples.

problems.problem: A trained model sits unused in a notebook
problems.approach: I wrap it in a small Streamlit app where people upload, record or paste and see the result, and in a tested FastAPI service when your own software must call it.

tradeoffs.title: Simple baseline or neural network
tradeoffs.text: A simple model such as Naive Bayes or a linear fit is quick to build and easy to explain. A neural network may add accuracy on audio or images. I build the simple one first and keep the stronger model only if the gap justifies the extra complexity.

tradeoffs.title: Test on new speakers or random samples
tradeoffs.text: A random split is quick, but it can flatter the result when one speaker or source appears on both sides. Splitting by speaker, customer or source gives a lower, fairer number. On your data I split that way where possible; my speech project used a random split.

tradeoffs.title: Fewer wrong blocks or fewer misses

case_study.summary: The AI audit finding generator is a standalone service at Claptek that turns short audit checklist notes into draft findings, three versions each. Code-level checks block any invented figure, date or owner, so the AI cannot add facts that were not in the auditor's note.
case_study.problem: Auditors spend hours turning terse checklist notes into well-formed findings. Simple AI drafting tends to invent figures and names. Both cost the business, because slow write-ups take time from real audit work. An invented figure, date or owner is worse, because someone may act on it or trust the report less.
case_study.approach: I built the drafting engine as a standalone FastAPI service (a Python web framework). An auditor's checklist note arrives with its verdict, and simple checks run before any AI time is spent. The service then finds similar past findings to use as writing examples. An AI language model that runs on Claptek's own servers writes the title, description, recommendation and severity, in three versions: short, balanced and detailed. Hard checks in code follow: any draft containing a figure, date or owner that is not in the auditor's note is rejected. Bulk mode drafts a whole workbook into a reviewable grid, and the client's audit product shows the three versions on its own edit screen.
architecture: One settings file per bank holds that bank's categories, example findings, pass and fail wording and required fields, so one codebase serves several banks.

Simple checks on the auditor's note run first, before any AI time is spent. A search step then finds similar past findings by keyword matching (TF-IDF, a keyword-weighting method) and passes them to the model as writing examples.
An AI language model on Claptek's own servers writes the title, description, recommendation and severity, using the auditor's note and the retrieved examples.

Code-level checks run on every reply. A draft is rejected if it holds a figure, date or owner that is not in the auditor's note. With no usable note, the service returns an outline with no specific facts for the auditor to complete.
Three versions of every finding: short, balanced and detailed, so the auditor can pick one and edit it.

Bulk mode: the user uploads a checklist workbook and maps its columns in the browser. Each row is drafted into a reviewable grid where it can be accepted, edited or rejected, then exported. A written summary report groups the findings by theme.

The client's audit product, built with Spring Boot (a Java framework) and React (a web screen library), gains a drafting action on its edit screen. Its backend gathers the item's details with one database query and sends them to this service, and the screen shows the three versions inline.
results: 0 invented facts across 27 checked draft versions, measured on real audit notes: none contained a figure, date or owner that was missing from the auditor's note.

Time per request fell from 7.9 minutes to 16.9 seconds, about 28 times faster. The cause was hidden extra processing in the way the system called the AI models. I fixed it and compared four candidate models, and accuracy stayed unchanged.
313 automated tests pass, and the code passes style and type checks.
The client's audit product team adopted the feature the day after handover. I had handed it over with a self-contained integration guide.

context: Audit teams record what they find in short checklist notes. Each note must become a formal finding with a title, a description, a recommendation and a severity rating. That write-up is slow, and a vague or wrong one leaves the people responsible unsure what to do. Faster, steadier drafting can give auditors time back for testing controls.

A good result is an auditor who types a short note and receives three draft findings in seconds, worded like earlier findings from the same bank. No draft adds a figure, date or owner that the auditor did not write. A person reviews every draft, and a whole checklist can be drafted in one pass.

challenges.title: Models invent details
challenges.text: Asked to write a finding, a language model fills gaps with plausible figures, dates and names. In an audit, one invented fact can mislead the people who must act on it.

challenges.title: Thin, uneven notes
challenges.text: Checklist notes are short, and each bank words things its own way. The service had to write a complete finding from very little, in the style of that bank's earlier findings.

challenges.title: A very slow response
challenges.text: At one point a single request took 7.9 minutes, which no auditor will wait for. The cause was buried in the way the system called the AI models, so I had to find it by testing.

challenges.title: Fitting a live product
challenges.text: The drafting had to work inside an audit product that another team owns, built with Spring Boot and React. The feature also had to be easy for that team to adopt.

owned: I designed and built the whole drafting service: the data formats, the search for past findings, the drafting steps, the code checks and the three-version output.
I built bulk mode: spreadsheet upload, column mapping, the reviewable grid, the export and the written summary report.
I built the connection to the client's Java and React audit product, including the database query that gathers each item's details and the drafting action on its edit screen.
I found the cause of the slowdown, fixed it and ran the four-model comparison of speed and draft quality.
I audited my own evaluation scripts, found measurement faults that had inflated the scores, and corrected them.
context: The service lives in a private client repository, so the code cannot be opened for inspection. This page rests on my own work, the test results and the measurements I took.
The audit product itself, with its Spring Boot and React code and its database, already existed and is owned by a separate product team. Other engineers built its other AI features.

decisions.title: Check in code, not in the prompt
decisions.choice: I enforce the rule that every figure, date and owner must appear in the auditor's note with a check in code, not only with an instruction in the prompt.
decisions.why: An instruction is a request that a model can ignore. A check in code rejects the draft every time, so the guarantee does not depend on how the model behaves that day.

decisions.title: Measure the slowdown before fixing it
decisions.choice: When requests took 7.9 minutes, I tested the AI model server directly instead of relying on its documentation, found the hidden extra processing, and compared four candidate models.
decisions.why: Guessing at fixes wastes time. Direct tests showed what the server really did. Once the hidden processing was off, time per request fell to 16.9 seconds and accuracy stayed unchanged.

decisions.title: Let the AI label, let code count
decisions.choice: In the summary report, the AI only labels each finding with a theme and an owner. Code does all the counting, and an owner label is accepted only if it appears in that row's own recommendation.
decisions.why: Charts built from AI-written numbers can look right and be wrong. Here code does the counting from the spreadsheet itself, and the AI only supplies the labels.

decisions.title: Reuse the product's own sign-in
decisions.choice: I made the drafting action use the audit product's existing sign-in, so it adds no new login to manage.
decisions.why: Drafts are built from confidential audit data. Reusing the product's existing access control keeps a single set of access rules to maintain.

limits: A person must still review every finding. The checks stop invented figures, dates and owners, but they cannot judge whether the wording or the severity rating is right.

The result of zero invented facts comes from 27 draft versions, which is a small sample, and the 16.9 seconds was measured on Claptek's own servers. I would measure both again on your notes and your hardware.
Finding similar past findings uses keyword matching, so it can miss an example that says the same thing in different words.
Today the service does not record who accepted or edited a draft, and it has no user roles of its own.

faq.q: Can AI write audit findings without making things up?
faq.a: Yes, when code checks every draft. Every figure, date or owner in a draft must appear word for word in the auditor's own note. A check rejects any draft that adds one. Across 27 checked draft versions it produced no invented facts, though a person still reviews each finding.

faq.q: Could the same approach work on my reports or tickets?
faq.a: The method is not specific to audit. It finds relevant evidence, uses an AI model hosted on your own machines and checks the output in code. I would first test it on a sample of your own documents to see how well it holds.

faq.q: Why did drafting get faster, from 7.9 minutes to 16.9 seconds?
faq.a: The cause was hidden extra processing: the AI model was doing long, hidden reasoning before each answer. I found it by testing the model server directly, fixed it and compared four candidate models on speed and draft quality. Time per request fell from 7.9 minutes to 16.9 seconds, about 28 times faster, with accuracy unchanged.

faq.q: What happens when the auditor's note is too short?
faq.a: The service does not guess. When there is no usable note, it returns an outline with no specific figures, dates or owners, and the auditor completes it. This stops a plausible but made-up story from being presented as fact, and it matches the rule enforced by the code checks.

faq.a: Yes. In bulk mode the user uploads a checklist workbook and maps its columns. Every row is drafted into a grid that looks like a spreadsheet, with all three versions of each finding. Reviewers accept, edit or reject each row, export the result and get a written summary report.

case_study.summary: This regulatory obligation extraction AI service at Claptek reads regulatory and compliance documents and returns a structured list of obligations. case_study.problem: Compliance teams build obligation lists by hand from long regulatory PDFs, and the page numbers an AI model gives for them cannot be trusted. Hand work is slow and must be repeated whenever a rule changes. Wrong page references send reviewers to the wrong place, so they may stop trusting the list and check everything again, which removes the time saved.
case_study.approach: I built the extraction in four steps. First, the document is split at page boundaries, and a merge step rejoins obligations that cross a break. Second, for each piece an AI language model on Claptek's own servers lists the obligations in a fixed format: an owner (who must act), a category from a fixed list, a risk or control tag and the section, plus the source sentence copied word for word. Third, code searches the PDF for that sentence and reads the page and highlight position from the document itself, instead of trusting a page number from the model. Fourth, a side-by-side preview shows each obligation beside its highlighted evidence.
architecture: The document is split at page boundaries, and a merge step joins obligations that cross a page break, so a duty is not cut in half.

For each piece, an AI language model hosted on Claptek's own servers extracts the obligations. It records each in a fixed format: an owner, a category from a fixed list, a risk or control tag and the section, so output stays consistent from one document to the next.

A locator finds each word-for-word quote in the PDF, using PyMuPDF (a PDF reading library), and reads the page number and highlight position from the document itself. I tested it on a set of reference records before connecting it to the live pipeline.

A side-by-side PDF preview (pdf.js, a browser PDF viewer) highlights the evidence for each obligation. For scanned pages that pdf.js cannot draw, the preview falls back to an image of the page at matching scale, so highlights stay in place.
Generation can be cancelled, which frees the model's memory and keeps the extracts already finished, so a long run resumes instead of restarting.

A second-read step, so far only tested in a controlled comparison and not yet in the live service, quotes the sentences that impose duties, drops every quote that is not found word for word in the PDF, and writes records from what is left.
A FastAPI backend (a Python web framework) serves the extraction, a React screen shows the list and the preview, and Docker packages the whole service for easy installation on a server.

challenges.title: Unreliable page numbers
challenges.text: An AI model can state a page number for each obligation, but those numbers were wrong 56% of the time. A reviewer sent to the wrong page loses trust in the whole list.

challenges.title: Long documents

decisions.title: Find the quote instead of trusting the page
decisions.choice: I ask the model to copy the source sentence word for word, then let code find that sentence in the PDF and read off the page and highlight position.
decisions.why: The model quoted text well but stated page numbers badly: its page numbers were wrong 56% of the time. Matching text is exact work for code, so each job goes to the tool that does it best.

decisions.title: Measure each speed-up before keeping it
decisions.choice: I profiled where processing time went, tested each proposed speed-up and kept only those that helped. Running two copies of the model side by side gave no net gain, so I did not use it.
decisions.why: Measurement showed the limit was how fast the machine can read the model's memory, which a second copy cannot widen. The changes that did help cut a six-document run from 80.4 to 60.0 minutes.

decisions.title: Check every quote against the source
decisions.choice: In the second-read step I tested, a first pass only quotes sentences that impose duties. Each quote is checked word for word against the PDF and dropped if it does not match.
decisions.why: A model can produce a plausible sentence that is not in the document. Dropping every unmatched quote lets the extra pass add coverage without adding invented quotes.

decisions.title: Test fairly before claiming a gain

faq.q: How do you extract obligations from regulatory documents?
faq.a: Split the document into pieces, then ask an AI language model to list each obligation and quote the source word for word. Code then finds that quote in the PDF to work out the page and highlight position, instead of trusting the page numbers the model gives. A person should still review the list.

faq.q: How do you keep the citations accurate?
faq.a: The AI returns a word-for-word quote, and code then finds that quote in the PDF to work out the page and highlight position. In the production data I measured, 97.2% of 1,266 records were located exactly. This replaced page numbers the model had often got wrong.

faq.q: Does it only work for one kind of regulation?
faq.a: No. It is not tied to one domain. The same process has read environmental permits, banking master directions, Basel III circulars and KYC rules without any domain-specific code. Other documents could work too, though I would first check results on a sample.

faq.q: What counts as an obligation in a regulatory document?
faq.a: An obligation is a duty the document places on someone: who must do what, and under which section. Examples are a duty to report, to keep records or to stay within a limit. The service lists each one with its owner, a category and a risk or control tag.

faq.q: What does the 97.2% figure actually measure?
faq.a: It measures how many of 1,266 production records could be linked to an exact passage in the source PDF, found by matching the model's word-for-word quote. Every record has a quote. The remaining 2.8% were not matched to an exact passage, so a reviewer should check those by hand.

faq.q: Does it replace the compliance reviewer?
faq.a: No. It gives a reviewer a head start: a structured list in which each duty sits beside its highlighted source sentence, so checking should be faster. faq.q: Where does the AI model run when it reads my documents?

case_study.summary: This text-to-SQL LLM (AI language model) assistant at Claptek runs on the bank's own servers. It turns plain-language reporting questions into working Oracle database queries (SQL) over a large core-banking database. My part was the accuracy measurement and the self-correction loop.
case_study.problem: The project's simple scoring rated the query writer at about 93% good. Actually running its queries showed that the share returning exactly the right rows was close to zero. Those scores checked whether the right tables were found and whether expected code values appeared in the query text, not whether the query returned the right rows. A team that trusts such a number ships wrong or empty reports and fixes the wrong things.
case_study.approach: I built the measurement first: a test that runs each generated query on a real database and compares the returned rows with a known-correct query. It scores strict row matches and also the recall and precision of the accounts returned. Then I added a retry loop, limited to two passes. When a query fails or returns no rows, the model is shown the real error and real values from the database, and asked to fix it. A glossary of real code values in the prompt makes filters use values that exist. The client ruled out a larger model and any retraining, so the gains had to come from the pipeline itself.
architecture: Table search, built by my teammate: it finds the right tables for each question in a core-banking database of 1,628 tables, using methods that include keyword search (BM25).
A language model (LLM) hosted on the bank's own servers with vLLM, a model-serving program, writes the Oracle query from the question and the chosen tables.
The query safety guard, built by my teammate with a SQL parser (sqlglot), checks each generated query before it runs. The test data was also my teammate's work.

The accuracy test, built by me, executes every generated query against a live database and compares its rows with those of a known-correct query. It reports strict row matches, accounts found (recall) and the correct share of results (precision).
The self-correction loop, built by me and limited to two passes: when a query errors or returns no rows, the model sees the real error and real column values, then revises the query.
A glossary of real code values from the database is added to the prompt, so filters use values that actually exist.
Hosted entirely on the bank's own servers, model included, so no outside AI service is involved. Generation is fixed at zero randomness to keep test runs repeatable.
results: After the self-correction loop was added, accounts found (recall) rose from 34% to 54% and the correct share of results (precision) from 19% to 27%, with no model change and no retraining. Both come from running the queries on a real database.
100% of 40 held-out test queries (kept apart from the ones used while building) were valid against the live database layout.
Stand-in scoring had put quality at about 93%. Running the queries put the exact-match rate close to zero, so every later gain is measured against a realistic baseline.
Generation is fixed at zero randomness to keep test runs repeatable, so a change in score points to a change in the system rather than to chance.
The whole pipeline, including the model, runs on the bank's own servers, so no data, prompt or usage record leaves the machine.

seo.h1: Text-to-SQL LLM assistant for core banking

h2.story: The problem: answers locked in a huge database
h2.arch: How a question becomes a checked SQL query
h2.ext: Where I would take this next

context: Banks and other large organisations keep their records in databases that can hold more than a thousand tables. In some of them only a few specialists can write SQL, the language used to read those tables, so each new report waits in a queue. A tool that turns a plain question into a correct query removes that wait, but only if people can trust what it returns.

A good result is an on-premise text-to-SQL assistant: it runs on the bank's own servers, so the bank's data stays inside the bank. It finds the right tables, writes a query that runs and returns the right accounts. Its quality is measured by running its queries on a real database, so a manager can see how often it is right before relying on it.

challenges.title: A very large database
challenges.text: A layout of 1,628 tables is too large to show a model in full for every question, so the few tables a question needs must be found first.

challenges.title: Scores that flatter
challenges.text: A query can look right and still return the wrong rows, or none. Only running it and comparing its rows with those of a query known to be correct shows the truth.

challenges.title: Invented code values
challenges.text: Many columns hold fixed codes, not words. A model that guesses a code writes a filter that looks right but matches nothing.

challenges.title: Strict client limits
challenges.text: The model had to run on the bank's own servers. A larger model and retraining were not allowed, so any gain had to come from how the system uses the model it had.

owned: The accuracy test that scores every generated query by running it and checking the rows it returns against the known-correct answer.
The scoring: strict row matching, plus recall and precision on the accounts a query returns, so partial success is visible.
The self-correction loop, limited to two passes, that shows the model the real error and real column values and asks for a fix.
The glossary of real code values added to the prompt, so filters use values that exist in the database.
Repeatable test runs: generation fixed at zero randomness, plus setup notes and a launcher so the pipeline could be run and measured on an ordinary developer machine.
context: A Claptek teammate built the table search over 1,628 tables, the query safety guard and the test data. I worked on the accuracy and correction side of a two-person effort.
No model was trained or tuned, and none was swapped. The client ruled out a larger model and retraining.
This is confidential client work. The database layout, the bank's data and the code stay private, so this page describes the design and the measured results only.

flow.label: Run and retry
flow.note: Real errors fed back, two passes

decisions.title: Score by running the queries
decisions.choice: I chose to judge quality by running each generated query on a real database, over scoring table matches and code strings in the query text.
decisions.why: Stand-in scores read about 93% while the share of queries returning exactly the right rows was close to zero. Only the rows a query returns show whether it does its job.

decisions.title: Fix the loop, not the model
decisions.choice: I chose a self-correction loop, limited to two passes, over asking for a larger model or retraining, which the client had ruled out.
decisions.why: The database itself tells the model what went wrong: a real error, or no rows. The loop is capped at two passes, so a hopeless query cannot retry forever.

decisions.title: Show the model real code values
decisions.choice: I chose to add a glossary of real code values to the prompt, over letting the model guess which codes a column holds.
decisions.why: Guessed codes look plausible but match nothing. With real values in front of it, the model writes filters that can find accounts.

decisions.title: Fix randomness for repeatable scores
decisions.choice: I chose to set the model's generation to zero randomness, over leaving it free, so test runs stay repeatable.
decisions.why: With random variation, a gain of a few points cannot be told from noise. Repeatable runs let each change be judged on its own.

limits: At 54% accounts found and 27% correct share of results, the output is a draft to review, not a finished report. A person should check a generated query before relying on its numbers.
Valid means a query fits the live database layout (100% of 40 held-out queries). It does not prove the rows are right. Recall and precision are the measures of that.

The figures come from one database with a core-banking layout, loaded with test data, and a prepared set of test questions. Another database or kind of question would need its own accuracy test before the numbers are trusted.
The gains came from how the system uses the model, inside the client's limits of no larger model and no retraining. I cannot say how far a bigger or tuned model would go.

use_cases.need: Analysts wait for a data team to write each query. Text-to-SQL for banking may shorten that wait, if the queries are checked and the assistant runs on the bank's own servers.
Reviewers want quick answers, such as which accounts meet a condition, drawn from live data, with the query shown so the answer can be checked and repeated.

use_cases.need: Hundreds or thousands of tables and few people who know them. Table search plus query writing can help, and an accuracy test shows whether it is good enough to use.
A demo looks good on simple scores, but nobody has run the queries. An accuracy test on real rows shows the true quality, and a correction loop may lift it without a new model.

Another compliance tool that turns hard-to-read material into checkable results, with accuracy measured against known-correct answers.

faq.q: What is text to SQL?
faq.a: Text to SQL means asking a database a question in everyday words and having an AI language model write the SQL query that answers it. The query is then run against the database. The hard parts are choosing the right tables and checking that the query is correct, which is why this project measures results by running queries.

faq.q: Is text to SQL safe for a bank database?
faq.a: It can be, with controls. Here the AI model runs on the bank's own servers, so no data, prompt or usage record leaves the machine. A query safety guard also checks queries before they run. My teammate built that guard; I built the accuracy test that compares returned rows with a correct query.

faq.q: How do you measure whether the generated query is right?
faq.a: By running it. The accuracy test executes the generated query on a real database and compares the rows with a known-correct query. Recall is the share of the right accounts the query returns; precision is the share of returned accounts that are right. These replaced simple scores that had overstated quality.

faq.q: Does any data leave the machine?
faq.a: No. The assistant runs fully on the bank's own servers, so no data, prompt or usage record leaves the machine. The AI model is hosted there too, so no online AI service is involved. For another project, the first step is to check that the servers are strong enough to run the model.

faq.q: Why did the first accuracy score say 93% when real accuracy was far lower?
faq.a: The first scores checked stand-ins: whether the right tables were found and whether the expected code values appeared in the query text. A query can pass both checks and still return wrong or empty results. Running the queries on a real database showed that exact row matches were close to zero, so I replaced the stand-ins.

faq.q: Which parts of the text-to-SQL assistant did you build yourself?
faq.a: I built the accuracy test and the self-correction loop, plus the code-value glossary in the prompt. A Claptek teammate built the table search, the query safety guard and the test data. It was a focused part of a two-person effort.

faq.q: Did you retrain or replace the AI model to raise accuracy?
faq.a: No. The client allowed no larger model and no retraining, so the model stayed as it was. The gain came from the self-correction loop: when a query failed or returned nothing, the model saw the real error and real column values and tried again, up to two passes. Recall rose from 34% to 54%.

case_study.summary: This healthcare RAG chatbot answers questions from six made-up healthcare policy documents. RAG means it looks up the right passages first and then writes the answer from them. It returns its source and a confidence label, and refuses out-of-scope questions instead of guessing.
case_study.problem: Healthcare answers must come from the right document. A confident wrong answer is worse than no answer. Policies are long, staff and patients ask about them again and again, and a wrong answer can mean a missed rule, a complaint or a compliance problem. An answer with no source also cannot be checked, so a reviewer cannot trust it.
case_study.approach: I built the chatbot as a small FastAPI service with three safety layers. First, a router works out what the user wants: a booking request, small talk or a policy question. Second, for policy questions the six documents are searched by meaning, and weak matches are dropped before the AI is called. Third, a strict instruction forces an exact fallback sentence when nothing relevant remains. Each answer drawn from the documents returns its source, a short excerpt and a confidence label. Settings and prompts live in plain files, and a chain of backup AI models keeps the service running if one is retired.
architecture: Six made-up policy documents (appointments, discharge, health-privacy rules, insurance, refills and telehealth) are read from plain text files and cut into chunks of 500 characters with an overlap of 50
Meaning-based search: sentence-transformers turns each chunk into numbers, stored in ChromaDB on disk. The model runs on the CPU and is baked into the Docker image, and the top 3 matches are used
A three-way router based on keywords: booking requests go to a mock scheduling tool, small talk to a friendly persona and everything else to the document chatbot
A similarity score threshold, set in the settings, drops weak matches before the AI is called. If nothing passes, a fixed "not found" reply is returned and the AI is not called at all

A strict instruction with an exact fallback sentence. Each answer drawn from the documents returns the source document, a short excerpt of the passage and a confidence label based on how many documents matched
A chain of backup Groq models: if one fails or is retired, the next is tried and the reply names the model that answered. Prompts and settings live in plain files
A FastAPI backend with health, ingest and ask endpoints, input limits and a request ID on the log lines of each request, a Streamlit chat screen and Docker packaging
results: Each answer drawn from the documents returns its source document, a short excerpt of the passage used and a confidence label
Out-of-scope questions are meant to get a fixed fallback sentence, not a guess: weak matches never reach the AI, and the strict prompt asks it to use the same sentence when the passages do not answer
The service keeps running when a hosted model is retired, without a code change, because the backup models are a setting
6 quick automated smoke tests check the health endpoint, input validation and document loading, and the backend is packaged in Docker
Each request gets a short ID that appears in its log lines and in the X-Request-ID response header, so one question can be followed through the logs
Re-loading unchanged documents does not create duplicate chunks, because each chunk gets a fixed ID built from its file name and text

A good result answers only from your own documents and shows the document and passage behind each answer. When the documents are silent, it says "not found" and points the person to the facility instead of guessing. Booking requests go to a scheduling tool (a mock in this prototype), and the prompts are plain text that a non-programmer can review. This project shows that behaviour on made-up policies.

challenges.title: Wrong answers cost more
challenges.text: In a healthcare setting a confident wrong answer is worse than no answer, so the chatbot must show its source and be able to refuse.

challenges.title: Telling questions apart
challenges.text: Booking requests, small talk and policy questions need different handling. A question such as "how are telehealth visits billed?" starts like small talk but is a policy question.

challenges.title: Keeping the AI inside the documents
challenges.text: A language model uses what it already knows unless told not to. The prompt had to forbid outside knowledge and medical advice, and weak matches had to be stopped before the model saw them.

challenges.title: Hosted models get retired
challenges.text: The settings file records two of the models I used as deprecated by the provider. The service needs a backup list that can change without code edits.

owned: All the application code: the FastAPI service, document loading and search, the router, the prompts and the Streamlit chat screen. Sole author, 28 commits.
The safety design: the score threshold, the exact fallback sentence, the strict prompts and the confidence label on every reply.
The settings and operations side: settings files, the backup model chain, request IDs in the logs and the Docker packaging.
The 6 quick automated tests, a written list of sample questions with expected answers and a script that calls the running server.
Fixes made along the way: repeat loading no longer creates duplicate chunks, the chat screen escapes text and a double-send bug is gone.
context: It was a take-home prototype. The six policy documents are made up and the scheduling tool is a mock, so nothing connects to a real clinic system or real patient data.
Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is a standard public pattern. ChromaDB, sentence-transformers and the hosted Groq model are existing tools that I configured and connected, not things I trained.
There is no live demo. The code is public, and the service runs locally or in Docker.

flow.label: Score check
flow.note: weak matches dropped, no AI call

decisions.title: Drop weak matches before the AI
decisions.choice: I filter retrieved passages by a similarity score and return a fixed "not found" reply, without calling the AI, when none pass.
decisions.why: The AI cannot misuse a passage it never sees, and an out-of-scope question costs no AI call. The threshold is a setting, so it can be made stricter without touching code.

decisions.title: Send unclear questions to the documents
decisions.choice: I used plain keyword rules to separate booking, small talk and policy questions. Anything unclear goes to document search, not to the chat persona.
decisions.why: Rules are easy to read and test. A misrouted policy question still meets the score threshold and the strict prompt, which is safer than a friendly reply that invents facts.

decisions.title: Keep prompts and settings in files
decisions.choice: Prompt wording sits in plain text files, and the main tunable values (models, threshold, chunk size, input limits, which websites may call the API) sit in settings, not in the code.
decisions.why: A reviewer who does not write code can read the prompt, changes show up as plain text differences, and tuning or swapping a model does not mean editing the code.

decisions.title: A chain of backup models
decisions.choice: I made the model list a setting. The service tries the main Groq model, then each backup in order, and every reply from the model names the model that answered.
decisions.why: Hosted models get retired. The settings file itself records two of the models I used as deprecated, and a backup list lets the service keep answering while I update it.

iteration.tried: My first version passed the top 3 passages to the AI whatever their score and relied on the prompt alone to refuse. Later I limited document search to questions containing a listed healthcare word, so anything else fell through to a canned greeting.
iteration.changed: I added a score threshold so weak matches never reach the AI, and made document search the default again for anything that is not a booking request or small talk. I then replaced the canned greetings with a persona prompt that may not invent facility facts.

limits: It reads only plain text files, runs on six made-up documents and has not been tried on real policy sets. It does not reload documents when a file changes, and old chunks stay until the collection is reset.

The repository keeps no scored check of answer quality. The 12 sample questions (plus 2 out-of-scope ones) are a manual list with expected answers, and the confidence label comes from how many documents matched. It is not a probability.
Routing uses keyword rules that can misread unusual wording. The booking tool is a mock, and there is no sign-in, no memory between questions and only a single language.
Questions and the few passages used are sent to a hosted AI service. A real deployment would need your own documents, a privacy and legal review, secured hosting and probably a private model.

use_cases.need: Front-desk staff and patients ask about refills, discharge limits, privacy and billing. A cited assistant answers from the facility's own policies and sends booking requests onward.
Policy holders ask what a plan covers or how to dispute a bill. The assistant answers from the plan documents and shows the passage behind each answer.
Staff ask about leave, expenses or conduct rules. An assistant that cites the handbook and admits when the handbook is silent is meant to cut down repeat questions to HR.
Staff must follow internal procedures and regulatory manuals. An assistant that answers with a source passage, or says "not found", lets a reviewer check every answer.

related.reason: Reads long policy and regulatory text and ties each obligation to a quoted source passage, so a reviewer can check it.
Lets people ask questions in everyday words, but over a bank database, with a safety guard on the queries it writes.
Puts an AI assistant in front of customers, on WhatsApp, with replies sent in the background and each conversation saved.

ask_prompts: How does it know when to say not found?
Can it run on our own policy documents?
What would a real deployment need?

extensions.title: Reading real document sets
extensions.benefit: I can build an intake step that reads PDFs and office documents into well-organised, labelled pieces.

extensions.title: Agents that use your tools
extensions.benefit: I can add agents that use your internal tools, such as real scheduling in place of the mock, lookups or ticket creation, with guarded permissions.

extensions.title: Better search and reranking
extensions.benefit: I can build hybrid search with a reranking step, so exact policy codes and reworded questions both find the right passage, and the best passage reaches the AI first, on infrastructure that scales.

extensions.title: Scored question set and stricter checks
extensions.benefit: I can build a set of test questions with scoring, plus stricter output checks, so answer quality is tracked over time.

extensions.title: Speed and usage dashboards
extensions.benefit: I can add tracking and dashboards for speed and AI usage, so every answer can be inspected end to end.

faq.q: How do you build a RAG chatbot?
faq.a: Cut your documents into chunks, turn each chunk into numbers a search index can compare, and store them. When a question arrives, find the best matching chunks, then ask an AI model to answer only from them. Here that used chunks of 500 with an overlap of 50, ChromaDB and the top 3 matches.

faq.q: How do you evaluate a RAG chatbot?
faq.a: Check three things. Does each answer cite the right source? Do out-of-scope questions get a plain "not found"? Are weak matches dropped before the AI is called? This prototype has 6 quick automated tests and a manual list of sample questions, but no scored check of answer quality. I would add that first for any real use.

faq.q: What happens when the answer is not in the documents?
faq.a: The chatbot says so. Weak matches are dropped before the AI is called, and the AI is told to use an exact fallback sentence when nothing relevant remains. That is how an out-of-scope question is meant to get a plain "not found" reply, pointing the person to the facility, instead of a confident guess.

faq.q: Does it use real patient data?
faq.a: No. It is a prototype built on six made-up policy documents and uses no real patient data. A real deployment would need the organisation's own documents, encrypted and access-controlled hosting, a privacy and legal review, agreements with any cloud provider that sees the data, and proper testing with the staff who will use it.

faq.q: Can this chatbot book real appointments?
faq.a: No. The scheduling tool is a mock. It picks a department and a day out of the question and returns four example time slots, marked as illustrative, with a note to call or use the patient portal to confirm. Real booking would mean connecting it to a real scheduling system, which I could build.

faq.q: Does the chatbot remember earlier questions in a chat?
faq.a: No. The chat screen shows the conversation so far, but the backend answers each question on its own, so a follow-up such as "and what about children?" carries no context. Adding memory is the improvement I listed for this project, and it needs care so old answers do not mix with new passages.

faq.q: What does the chatbot send to the hosted AI service?
faq.a: At question time, only the last step goes online. The model that searches the documents runs on the server's own processor. For each question, the question text and the few matching passages are sent to the hosted Groq model, which writes the answer. For private data, a model on the organisation's own servers would be used.

projects.title: Scam-Catching AI Honeypot
projects.tagline: An Artificial Intelligence (AI) victim that keeps scammers talking and takes notes.
projects.description_short: A counter-scam system: an AI plays an easily fooled target, keeps scammers talking and records the UPI payment IDs, links and phone numbers they reveal.
projects.role: Co-author with Prasanna Patil. I added the filter that blocks prompt-injection attempts (tricks that try to hijack the AI) and the request limiter. I moved the AI from Gemini to Groq. I also rewrote the persona prompts and detail-extraction patterns, and reworked parts of the dashboard. Prasanna wrote the first version, the Docker setup and the README.
projects.card_blurb: An AI plays an easily fooled victim, keeps scammers chatting and logs the payment IDs, links and phone numbers they reveal.

case_study.summary: This AI scam honeypot is a counter-scam system co-built with Prasanna Patil. An AI plays an easily fooled victim, keeps scammers talking and records the UPI payment IDs, links and phone numbers they reveal. A rule-based selector changes its style as scam risk grows, and a live dashboard shows what it collects.
case_study.problem: A blocked scammer just tries the next number, and nobody learns how the scam works. A bot that keeps scammers busy protects real people for as long as the chat lasts and leaves a record of exactly what the scammers ask for. Without that record, a fraud team may learn about a scam only after someone reports a loss.
case_study.approach: The system is a FastAPI service with a React dashboard. It scores every incoming message for scam signals. Separately, a rule-based selector sets the bot's style: passive at first, vulnerable once a risk level (raised by shouting or very short messages) passes a limit, and stalling once enough details are collected. A persona prompt drives an AI model on Groq, which writes each reply from the last 10 messages. Pattern matching pulls out payment and contact details, and the live dashboard shows them. Prasanna Patil wrote the first version. I added the safety layer, moved the AI to Groq and rewrote the persona prompts and the link and phone patterns.
architecture: Intake, from Prasanna's first version. A FastAPI endpoint takes a conversation ID and a message, as text or a small JSON object, and needs an access key in a request header. Interactive API documentation (Scalar) is served alongside it.

Safety layer, added by me. A filter checks for five known injection phrases and, on a match, sends a canned confused reply and does not store the message. A limiter gives each visitor address 1 request per second, with bursts of 5, and refuses the rest with HTTP 429.

Scam scoring, from Prasanna's first version. 21 keyword patterns, such as lottery, tax, UPI and arrest, each add 0.2 to a message's score. At 0.7 or more the conversation is flagged, and the flag stays. The bot replies either way.

Style selection, from Prasanna's first version. A rule-based selector picks one of four styles: passive on the first message, engaged after that, vulnerable once a running risk level passes 0.6, and stalling once more than three details are collected. Shouting or very short messages raise the risk level.

Persona, memory and model, shared. Each conversation is kept in server memory under its ID. A persona prompt that I rewrote, plus the current style, goes to a model hosted on Groq with the last 10 messages. I moved this step from Gemini to Groq.

Detail extraction, first version by Prasanna, link and phone patterns widened by me. Patterns pick UPI IDs, links and phone numbers out of each incoming message. Each record keeps its type, value, a fixed confidence (0.9, 0.95 and 0.8) and the turn it appeared in.

Dashboard and delivery. Prasanna built the React dashboard, the Docker setup and the README. The dashboard shows the chat, the status, the current style, the collected details and the matched signals. I made small changes to it.
results: The bot's style changes automatically: passive on the first message, engaged from the second, vulnerable once the risk level passes 0.6, and stalling once more than three details are collected.

UPI IDs, links and phone numbers are stored as structured threat records: type, value, a fixed confidence (0.9, 0.95 and 0.8) and the turn found. These confidence values are set in the code, not measured accuracy.
Each visitor address is limited to 1 request per second, with bursts of 5. A request over the limit gets HTTP 429.
The persona sees the last 10 messages for each reply, while the server keeps the whole conversation in memory under its ID.
A live dashboard shows warning signals, the current style and the details collected, next to the chat window where the tester plays the scammer.
Contribution record: of 19 changes in the shared history, I wrote 4 and merged 4 pull requests. The other 11 are Prasanna's, counted from the commit log.

seo.title: AI Scam Honeypot Agent Case Study | Shaunak Chorge
seo.description: Case study: an AI that plays an easily fooled target, keeps scammers talking and records the UPI payment IDs, links and phone numbers they reveal.
seo.h1: AI scam honeypot that keeps scammers talking

h2.story: The problem: scammers waste real people's time
h2.arch: How the AI plays the victim
h2.ext: What I can add for your project

context: Banks, payment apps, telecom firms and messaging platforms face the same pattern. Scammers message many people at once, and each reply, click or payment costs a real person money and costs the business support time and trust. Blocking one number changes little, because the scammer moves to the next. What is usually missing is a record of how the scam works.

A good result is a safe place where a scammer can be kept talking for as long as possible, while the business collects the payment IDs, links and phone numbers the scammer shares. That record can feed block lists and investigations. This case study covers a hackathon prototype of that idea, built with a co-builder, and says clearly who built which part.

challenges.title: Staying believable
challenges.text: A scammer may test whether a bot is on the other end. The persona must reply in short, casual messages, stay in character for many turns and never admit to being an AI.

challenges.title: Hostile and abusive input
challenges.text: The other side is a scammer, so messages may try to hijack the AI, for example with "ignore previous instructions", or flood the server. A cheap first line of defence must act before any message reaches the model.

challenges.title: Messy payment details
challenges.text: UPI IDs, links and phone numbers can be written in many forms, such as a link with no "http" or a number with spaces. A pattern wide enough to catch them will also catch some look-alikes.

challenges.title: Two builders, one codebase
challenges.text: The 18 build commits in the shared history fall on two days. Two people worked on one codebase, so I used separate branches that were merged back through pull requests.

owned: A filter for prompt-injection phrases that answers with a canned confused reply, and a request limiter of 1 per second per visitor with bursts of 5.
Moving the reply model from Gemini to Groq, including how the last 10 messages are passed to it.
Rewriting the persona prompts, and the patterns that pick out phone numbers and web addresses.
Small dashboard changes: it now sends the access key and no longer names a model, and its build tools moved to Vite 6.
context: Prasanna Patil wrote the first version: scam scoring, the style selector, conversation memory, the detail extractor, the API and the first dashboard, plus the Docker setup and the README.
It is a hackathon prototype. In the shared commit history, 18 of the 19 changes fall on two days; the last, a licence file, came months later.

flow.label: Score and style
flow.note: signals, risk, one of four styles

flow.label: Dashboard
flow.note: live view of chat and details

decisions.title: Answer injection attempts with a canned reply
decisions.choice: When a message contains an injection phrase, the bot sends one of four canned confused replies and skips the AI model, instead of returning an error.
decisions.why: The injected text never reaches the model, and the other side still gets an ordinary reply, not an error. A keyword list is only a first line of defence, as the limits section says.

decisions.title: A token bucket for the request limit
decisions.choice: I used a token bucket (an allowance that refills over time) for each visitor address: 1 request per second, with bursts of 5.
decisions.why: A quick burst of messages passes, but a sustained flood does not. The limiter is small, needs no extra service, and refused requests get the standard HTTP 429 answer.

decisions.title: A short, casual, slightly lazy persona
decisions.choice: I rewrote the persona prompt so the bot plays a human, replies in one or two casual sentences, never admits to being an AI and is not too eager.
decisions.why: The active persona is a student short of cash and keen on quick money; an elderly persona is defined but not used. The prompt aims for a believable young person, sceptical by default, which suits keeping a scammer talking.

decisions.title: Wider patterns for links and numbers
decisions.choice: I widened the link pattern to catch web addresses without "http", and added capture of 10-digit and country-code phone numbers.
decisions.why: A strict pattern misses bare addresses and plain numbers. The cost is false matches, such as an email's domain read as a link or any ten-digit number read as a phone number, so the details are leads for a person to check, not verified facts.

limits: Detection is keyword based, not semantic. A message needs at least four of the 21 patterns to be flagged, so honest messages can be flagged and new tricks missed. It has not been measured on labelled conversations.

The injection filter is a keyword list, so it is a first line of defence, not a full defence. The limiter and the conversation memory live in server memory, so they reset on restart and do not work across several servers.

Patterns can misread: an email address can be recorded as a UPI ID, and a repeated detail is stored again each time. The collected details are not sent anywhere, so there is no report to a bank or an authority.

This is a hackathon prototype. The repository has no automated test suite, the sample access key and server address are written into the demo code, and if the AI provider fails the reply is an error message.

use_cases.who: A bank or payments fraud team
use_cases.need: It wants a safe decoy that scammers can be steered to, so it can collect the payment IDs, links and numbers they use as leads for block lists and investigations.

use_cases.who: A messaging or telecom trust team
use_cases.need: It wants to study how scam scripts unfold, what scammers ask for and how long they stay engaged, without putting a real customer in the conversation.

use_cases.who: A university or security research lab
use_cases.need: It needs a controlled decoy to study scammer behaviour, with each message, the bot's style and the collected details visible on one dashboard.
It wants real examples of how current scams escalate, to train staff and warn customers. That would need conversations saved to a database, which this prototype does not do.

related.reason: Both fight unwanted and fraudulent messages: the classifier filters them out, while the honeypot keeps scammers busy and records what they reveal.
Both run automated chat conversations with AI replies and keep a history for each user or session.
Both help organisations spot and counter digital deception before it harms real people.

How does the bot decide what to say next?
What does it record, and does it report scammers?

extensions.benefit: I can add a trained detector alongside the pattern rules and measure it on a labelled set of conversations.

extensions.title: Memory and tools for the agent
extensions.benefit: I can give the persona longer memory and tools, such as looking up earlier chats with the same sender.

extensions.title: Searchable conversation store
extensions.benefit: I can save every conversation and collected detail so analysts can search and export them, or send them to a fraud team's system.

extensions.title: Attack-testing suite
extensions.benefit: I can build automated tests of injection attempts and stronger output checks, going beyond the keyword filter.

extensions.title: Tracking and analytics dashboards
extensions.benefit: I can add dashboards for chat length, detail-collection rate and AI response time.

faq.q: What is an AI honeypot?
faq.a: An AI honeypot is a decoy that looks like an easy target, so attackers waste their time on it and reveal how they work. Here an AI persona plays a victim in a chat and keeps a scammer talking. It records the payment IDs, links and phone numbers the scammer shares, ready for study.

faq.q: How do you create an AI agent?
faq.a: Give the AI a clear job, a way to read the situation and rules for what it may do. In this project each message is scored for scam signals. A rule-based selector picks one of four styles, and an AI persona on Groq writes the reply. Pattern matching then saves the details it collects.

faq.q: Who built which part?
faq.a: It was co-built with Prasanna Patil. Prasanna wrote the first version, the Docker setup and the README. I added the injection filter and the request limiter, moved the AI from Gemini to Groq, and rewrote the persona prompts and the link and phone patterns. Of the 19 changes in the shared history, I wrote 4 and merged 4.

faq.q: How well does it resist prompt injection?
faq.a: It has a keyword filter for five phrases, such as "ignore previous instructions", and a request limiter. On a match, the bot sends a canned reply and the text never reaches the model. That is a first line of defence, not a complete solution, because a determined attacker can reword a trick. A real project would add attack tests.

faq.q: What details does the honeypot record from a scammer?
faq.a: It records UPI IDs, links and phone numbers found in the scammer's messages. Each record keeps its type, the value, a fixed confidence level and the turn where it appeared. It does not look for bank account numbers or card numbers. Records stay in server memory until the server restarts, and the dashboard shows them as they arrive.

faq.q: How does the bot remember a conversation?
faq.a: Each conversation is stored in server memory under its ID, with every message, the scam score, the current style and the details found. For each reply the AI model sees the last 10 messages. Because the store is in memory, a restart clears everything. A real version would use a database.

faq.q: Does the honeypot report scammers anywhere?
faq.a: No. Apart from the request to the AI model, it makes no outgoing calls. The collected details stay in the reply it returns, in server memory and on the dashboard. Sending them to a fraud team, a block list or a case system would be an addition I can build if a project needs it.
