projects.title: CCTV Crime and Crowd Analytics
projects.tagline: Three watchers for camera footage.
projects.description_short: A Smart India Hackathon team project that watches camera footage three ways: crowd-limit alerts, crime labels from video frames and face recognition, with evidence frames saved to a database.
projects.role: Member of the Smart India Hackathon team. Co-built with Prasanna Patil.
projects.card_blurb: Smart India Hackathon team prototype: crowd-limit alerts, crime labels from video frames and face recognition, as three separate modules.

case_study.summary: CCTV video analytics in Python: this Smart India Hackathon team prototype watches camera footage three ways. A crowd counter raises a limit alert, a crime module labels sampled video frames and a face module recognises enrolled people. The crowd and crime modules save evidence frames to MongoDB and send WhatsApp alerts. Co-built with Prasanna Patil.
case_study.problem: Public-safety teams cannot watch every camera at once. Overcrowding, violent incidents and known persons of interest slip past exactly when attention matters most. The cost is a slower response, more risk to the people on site and more damage or liability for the venue, because a team that checks screens by eye can only react after someone happens to notice.
case_study.approach: The prototype splits monitoring into three separate modules. The crowd module removes the video background to find moving shapes, tracks each shape and counts people crossing two virtual lines, then raises an alert at a set limit. The crime module checks one frame every 3 seconds with a pre-trained Vision Transformer (ViT, an image-classification model) that returns one of 14 labels. The face module finds faces with Haar cascades (a classic face finder) and names them with an LBPH matcher (a classic face-matching method), after a small tool enrols the people to look for. The crowd and crime modules save evidence frames to MongoDB and send alerts through Twilio WhatsApp. Flask pages show the latest saved frame.
architecture: Crowd module: OpenCV background subtraction (MOG2) finds moving shapes, and a simple tracker gives each one an ID. Two virtual lines count people crossing in each direction. At the limit of 12 it saves the frame, beeps twice, sends a WhatsApp alert and starts the review page server.

Crime module: a pre-trained Vision Transformer, published on the Hugging Face model hub as UCF_Crime, labels one frame every 3 seconds with one of 14 UCF-Crime labels: 13 incident types, such as Fighting or Robbery, and a normal label.

Face module: Haar cascades locate faces in a webcam image. A small tkinter window enrols a person by saving cropped 200 by 200 pixel photos, and an LBPH matcher then shows a name, or "not recognized", on screen.

Evidence store: the crowd and crime modules save each evidence frame as an image in MongoDB, a database. The crime module keeps the label with the frame and skips a frame whose exact pixels were already stored.
Review pages: two small Flask pages show the latest saved frame from MongoDB, one for crowd alerts and one for crime labels, where the label sits above the picture.

Alerts: the Twilio WhatsApp API sends a short text when the crowd limit is reached, carrying the ID of the saved frame, and one text when the crime module finishes a video. Neither message includes the picture.

Inputs and settings: the crowd and crime modules read a video file chosen in a file dialog, and the face tool reads a webcam. The crowd limit and the crime sampling interval are plain variables in the scripts.
results: Three separate monitoring modules: a crowd counter, a crime labeller and a face recogniser.
The crime model has 14 labels, 13 incident types and a normal label, and the code checks one frame every 3 seconds. Both are settings read from the code, not measured accuracy.
On the sample crowd clip in the repository, the counter reached its limit of 12 crossings. The saved frame and a count log with 12 entries are kept with the code.
The crowd and crime modules save evidence frames and labels to MongoDB, with Flask pages that show the latest saved frame.
The team won the college's internal round of the Smart India Hackathon.

seo.title: CCTV Video Analytics with Python | Shaunak Chorge
seo.description: Case study: a Smart India Hackathon team project that watches one CCTV video three ways: crowd-limit alerts, crime labels and face recognition.
seo.h1: CCTV video analytics in Python: crowds, crime and faces

h2.story: The problem: too much footage, too few eyes
h2.arch: Crowd alerts, crime labels and face matching
h2.results: What the prototype shows and does not show
h2.ext: What I can build for your cameras

context: Shops, event venues, campuses and transport hubs often run more cameras than their security staff can watch at once. Crowds build past a safe size, fights start and people who should not be on site walk in, often while a screen goes unwatched. Software that watches the footage, sends a short alert and keeps the picture behind it is meant to help a small team spot these moments sooner.

A good result is an alert that a person can trust and check. It says what was seen, keeps the frame behind it and does not flood the team with false alarms. For a buyer, that means measuring each alert type on their own footage before relying on it, and setting privacy rules before any face data is stored.

challenges.title: Overlapping people in a crowd
challenges.text: People who walk close together merge into one moving shape. The sample crowd clip in the repository is a dense street scene, so counting by shapes is rough and every count is an estimate.

challenges.title: Judging crime from a still frame
challenges.text: The classifier sees one picture every 3 seconds, with no sense of movement, so the context that makes an event a crime is often missing. Its labels are hints for a person to check.

challenges.title: Alerts that come with evidence
challenges.text: A bare alarm is hard to trust or act on. Each alert needs a saved frame and, for crime, a label to check. That means storing images and reading them back for review.

challenges.title: Faces are personal data
challenges.text: Recognising a person means keeping their face photos. That raises consent, retention and access questions that this prototype does not yet handle.

owned: Worked as a member of the Smart India Hackathon team and co-built the prototype with Prasanna Patil.
Shared in the team's win of the college's internal round of the Smart India Hackathon.
Kept a copy of the team's repository on my account. It was first uploaded from my co-builder's account, my only commit is a README line, and I claim no sole credit.
context: The code was uploaded in one batch, so its history cannot show who wrote which module. I describe all three modules as shared team work.
The crime classifier is a published model loaded by name from the Hugging Face model hub. The repository holds no training code for it.
The crowd counter's tracker and line counting follow a public people-counter example, and the face tool follows public OpenCV tutorials. Some crowd page buttons and lights are placeholders.

flow.label: Analyse
flow.note: Crowd, crime or face; face ends here

flow.label: Save
flow.note: Crowd and crime frames to MongoDB

flow.label: Alert
flow.note: Crowd and crime texts via Twilio

decisions.title: Three separate modules, not one pipeline
decisions.choice: Crowd counting, crime labelling and face recognition are separate programs, each with its own input and settings. The crowd and crime programs each have their own review page.
decisions.why: Each can be run, tested and replaced on its own, and a fault in one does not stop the others. The cost is that they do not yet share one feed or one dashboard.

decisions.title: A published crime model, not a new one
decisions.choice: The crime module loads a Vision Transformer published on the Hugging Face model hub as UCF_Crime, with the 14 UCF-Crime labels. The repository holds no training code.
decisions.why: It gives usable labels without collecting and labelling footage first. The trade-off is that its accuracy on a buyer's own cameras is unknown until it is measured.

decisions.title: Classic OpenCV methods for people and faces
decisions.choice: The prototype finds people by background subtraction and counting lines, from a public example, and faces by Haar cascades with an LBPH matcher, rather than a trained detector.
decisions.why: These methods are light, need no training data for counting and only a few dozen photos per person for faces. The trade-off is weaker results in dense crowds, poor light and side-on faces.

decisions.title: Evidence frames stored in MongoDB
decisions.choice: Each alert keeps its frame as an image in MongoDB, and a Flask page reads back the latest one for a reviewer.

limits: No accuracy was measured. Counts, crime labels and face matches were not tested against labelled footage, so the prototype shows the idea and the working parts, not a reliability figure.

faq.q: What is video analytics in CCTV?
faq.a: Video analytics is software that watches camera footage and reports what it sees, such as how many people are in a place, unusual events or known faces. This prototype has three separate modules: crowd counting with an alert, crime labels from sampled frames and face recognition. The crowd and crime modules save their evidence to a database.

faq.q: How accurate is the crime classifier?
faq.a: I do not quote an accuracy figure, because I did not measure one on labelled footage. The module uses a pre-trained Vision Transformer with 14 UCF-Crime labels and checks one frame every 3 seconds. A real project would start by measuring it on footage from your own site, then tune the alert rules.

faq.q: Did you build all of it yourself?
faq.a: No. It was a team project, co-built with Prasanna Patil for the Smart India Hackathon. I was a member of the team and I do not claim sole credit for any module. The code was uploaded in one batch from his account, so its history cannot show who wrote what. The team won the college's internal round.

faq.q: How does the crowd counter decide when to raise an alert?
faq.a: It removes the video background to find moving shapes, tracks each one and counts people who cross a virtual line. When the count reaches the limit, set to 12 in the code, it saves the frame to MongoDB, beeps, sends a WhatsApp text and stops. The limit counts crossings downward, not people present at once.

faq.q: How does the face recognition part work?
faq.a: A small window enrols a person by saving cropped photos from a webcam. OpenCV's LBPH recogniser, a classic face-matching method, is then trained on those photos. Haar cascades find faces in the live image and the screen shows a name or "not recognized". It follows public tutorials, sends no alerts and keeps no evidence frames, only the enrolment photos.

faq.q: Which crimes can the model label?
faq.a: The model has 14 labels: Abuse, Arrest, Arson, Assault, Burglary, Explosion, Fighting, Road accidents, Robbery, Shooting, Shoplifting, Stealing, Vandalism and a normal-video label. It picks one label for each sampled frame, with no confidence cut-off, so a label is a hint for a person to check and not a finding.

faq.q: Is this prototype ready for a real control room?
faq.a: No. It is a hackathon prototype made of desktop scripts that run on one computer and read video files or a webcam. Settings sit inside the code and there are no automated tests. A real deployment would need network camera input, accuracy tests on your footage, alert rules, privacy controls and monitoring.

projects.title: Speech Emotion Recognition
projects.tagline: Hear the mood in a voice clip, live from the mic.
projects.description_short: A neural network that labels seven emotions in speech, trained on four public datasets: 93.87% on a random 20% test split, with live microphone input.
projects.role: I adapted a public training recipe from Kaggle, retrained and tested it on four datasets, then wrote the live-input notebook and the Streamlit dashboard.
projects.card_blurb: Detects seven emotions in a voice clip with a neural network: 93.87% on a random test split, with live microphone input.

case_study.summary: This speech emotion recognition project is a neural network (a 1-D CNN, which reads audio as a sequence) that labels seven emotions in speech clips. It was trained on four public datasets and scored 93.87% on a random 20% test split. It comes with live microphone input and a web dashboard.
case_study.problem: Emotion lives in tone, pitch and energy, not in the words, so a text-based model is the wrong tool. A transcript of a call keeps the words and loses the tone, so an angry caller and a calm one can read the same. A team that works from text alone can miss the very signal that shows which customers need a person.
case_study.approach: I started from a public training recipe on Kaggle and adapted it. The four datasets are merged into 12,162 labelled clips, and each clip becomes four versions: the original plus three altered copies, giving 48,648 examples. librosa turns each example into 2,376 numbers that describe the sound of the voice. A five-block neural network then learns seven emotions from those numbers. I tested it on a random 20% of the examples and serve it through notebooks, including live microphone input, and a Streamlit dashboard.
architecture: Four public datasets (RAVDESS, CREMA-D, TESS and SAVEE) merged into 12,162 clips, with RAVDESS calm recordings counted as neutral, so every clip has one of seven emotion labels.
Each clip is read as a 2.5-second window and made into four versions: the original, one with added noise, one pitch-shifted and one pitch-shifted with noise. That gives 48,648 samples.
librosa audio features: zero-crossing rate, energy and MFCCs (numbers that describe the sound of a voice), 2,376 numbers per sample, put on one scale with a scaler fitted on the training data only.

A five-block 1-D neural network (convolution, normalisation and pooling) with steps to prevent overfitting (memorising the training clips), then a 512-unit layer and a seven-way output. It has 7.19 million parameters.
Training uses the Adam optimiser for 20 passes over a random 80% of the samples (38,918), in batches of 64. The other 20% (9,730) is the test set.
A notebook for live microphone input: it records 2.5 seconds at a time, extracts the same features, scales them and prints the predicted emotion, then repeats until stopped.
A Streamlit dashboard: upload a WAV file or record, then see the emotion, its confidence, class probabilities and waveform and spectrogram views.
results: Seven emotions are recognised: angry, disgust, fear, happy, neutral, sad and surprise.
93.87% accuracy and a weighted F1 score of 0.94 (one number that balances missed cases against false alarms) on a random 20% test split of 9,730 samples.
Per-emotion F1 scores run from 0.92 (sad) to 0.97 (surprise), measured on the same test split.

The score is for the final model, the one that is saved and used. An earlier training pass reached 95.24% on the same split; I quote the final figure because picking the best pass would flatter the model.
Caution: the test split can hold altered copies of clips that were also used in training, so the score does not show how it performs on new speakers.
Live microphone detection runs in a notebook and in the Streamlit dashboard. It has not been scored, so no accuracy figure is claimed for live speech.

h2.story: The problem: finding the mood in a voice
h2.ext: What I can add for your recordings

context: Teams that record customer calls or voice messages cannot listen to every recording. Mood can show in the voice as well as in the words, so a caller who sounds angry or frightened can be missed by a search of the transcript. A model that labels emotion from audio could help a team decide which recordings deserve a person's time.

A good result is a model that labels the emotion in a short clip, shows how sure it is, and comes with a score that says how it was measured and what it does not prove. This project is that first step, on public recordings of speakers. Using it on real calls would need a fresh test on that team's own audio.

challenges.title: Four datasets, one label set
challenges.text: The four public datasets cover emotions differently: CREMA-D has no surprise clips and RAVDESS has a separate calm label. They had to be merged into one set of seven labels, with calm counted as neutral.

challenges.title: Uneven emotion examples
challenges.text: Surprise has 652 clips, against 1,923 for each of angry, disgust, fear, happy and sad. The model sees far fewer examples of it, and the test set holds only 505 surprise samples.

challenges.title: Long training time
challenges.text: The network has 7.19 million parameters. Its 20 training passes took about ten hours in total, roughly half an hour each, so every retrain is a planned run, not a quick test.

challenges.title: A score that can flatter
challenges.text: Altered copies of one clip can sit on both sides of the split, the same speakers appear on both sides, and the test split doubled as the validation set. The score can therefore overstate how well it handles new voices.

owned: Adapting the public Kaggle training recipe and retraining the network on the four merged datasets.
Testing the retrained model on a random 20% split, reading the per-emotion scores and stating the limits of that test plainly.
The inference notebook: it loads the saved model, predicts from an audio file and listens to the microphone in a live loop.
The Streamlit dashboard: upload or record audio, then see the emotion, its confidence and a probability bar for every class, plus waveform and spectrogram views.
Saving the model design, scaler and label encoder as files and publishing the notebooks in a public repository.
context: The training recipe (data merge, audio altering, features and the 1-D network) comes from a public Kaggle notebook. I adapted and retrained it. The model design is not my own invention.
The four datasets are public collections of speakers reading fixed sentences or words in each emotion. I recorded no audio, and no real calls or customers were involved.
The dashboard is a local prototype. The public repository holds the notebooks, the model design and the preprocessing files, not the dashboard or the large trained weights.

decisions.title: Adapt a public recipe
decisions.choice: I chose to adapt a public Kaggle training recipe over designing a network from scratch.
decisions.why: The recipe already covered the data merge, audio altering and feature steps. My effort went into retraining it, testing it honestly and making it usable live from a microphone.

decisions.title: Merge four datasets
decisions.choice: I trained on four merged datasets (RAVDESS, CREMA-D, TESS and SAVEE) rather than on one.
decisions.why: Together they hold 12,162 clips from 121 speakers, by the datasets' own descriptions. One dataset alone can have as few as two speakers and one recording style.

decisions.title: Keep four versions of each clip
decisions.choice: I kept the recipe's four versions of each clip (original, noise, pitch shift, pitch shift with noise) rather than training on the original clips alone.
decisions.why: More varied examples make it harder for the network to lean on one recording's quirks. The cost is that copies of one clip can fall on both sides of the split, so the score does not prove new-voice accuracy.

decisions.title: Report the final model
decisions.choice: I report the score of the final saved model (93.87%) rather than the best single training pass (95.24%).
decisions.why: Both numbers come from the same test split, and choosing the best pass by its test score would flatter the model. The final model is the one that is saved and used.

limits: The test is not fully independent. Altered copies of one clip, and the same speakers, appear on both sides of the split, and the test split doubled as the validation set during training. Accuracy on new voices is likely to be lower.

Every clip is a speaker reading fixed words or sentences in a requested emotion. Real calls bring background noise, phone-quality audio, other languages and mixed feelings, none of which this model has been tested on.
It reads a 2.5-second window and picks one of seven labels. Longer speech, changing emotion and labels outside the seven are not handled, and live microphone use has not been scored.
The dashboard is a local prototype, and the large trained weights are not in the public repository, so a real build would start from a fresh, tested package with its own accuracy check.

use_cases.need: Teams that record customer calls could use emotion labels to choose which calls a person should listen to first, once the model has been tested on their own recordings.
An app that asks people to speak could show a mood signal for a person to review, never as a diagnosis, after a careful test on its own users' voices.

use_cases.who: Voice assistant and phone menu teams
use_cases.need: A voice assistant or phone menu could hand a caller who sounds upset to a person sooner, if the model is tested on that product's microphones and callers.
Anyone studying speech can use the same pipeline as a baseline: merge public datasets, extract features, train a network and report scores with their caveats.

faq.q: What is speech emotion recognition?
faq.a: Speech emotion recognition is software that listens to a voice clip and guesses the emotion from tone, pitch and energy rather than the words. This project labels seven emotions: angry, disgust, fear, happy, neutral, sad and surprise. It reads numbers that describe the sound from the audio and passes them to a neural network.

faq.q: How accurate is speech emotion recognition?
faq.a: In this project, 93.87% on a random 20% test split of 9,730 samples. That figure does not cover new speakers, because altered copies of one clip can land on both sides of the split. Accuracy on unseen voices is likely to be lower, so a real project would first measure it by splitting speakers apart.

faq.q: Can it work with my own recordings?
faq.a: It can be retrained on your recordings if they are labelled with the emotions you care about. Quality depends on the microphone, the language and the number of speakers. I would first test it on a sample of your audio and report how well it holds.

faq.q: How much of the speech emotion model did you design yourself?
faq.a: The network design is not mine. The training recipe is a public Kaggle notebook, which I adapted and retrained on four datasets. My own work is the testing and its stated limits, the live microphone notebook, the Streamlit dashboard and the saved model files, and I say so plainly on this page.

faq.q: Why does the repository quote 97.25% when this page says 93.87%?
faq.a: The repository README and the notebook's file name quote 97.25%, but the notebook's own output never shows that figure. The saved model scores 93.87% on the 9,730-sample test split, so I report that number, with its caveats. The README figure is not supported by the notebook's output, so this page does not use it.

faq.q: Does it work in real time from a microphone?
faq.a: A notebook records 2.5 seconds at a time, extracts the same features, scales them and prints an emotion, then repeats until stopped. The dashboard can record 1.5 to 5 seconds and shows a bar for each emotion. Neither has been scored for accuracy on live speech, so treat live output as a demo.

faq.q: How long does it take to train a speech emotion model?
faq.a: Here, the 20 training passes took about ten hours in total, roughly half an hour each, and extracting features from all 12,162 clips took about two minutes spread over 20 processor cores. Time depends on the computer and the data, so I would size a new project on a sample first.

projects.description_short: A college team project: a small neural network scores each video frame as real or fake, with a Streamlit app, confidence chart and PDF report. 74.16% test accuracy.
projects.role: Member of a three-person college team. The repository is published from my account.
projects.card_blurb: Scores each frame of a video as real or fake, with a web app and PDF report. College project, 74.16% accuracy.

case_study.summary: This deepfake video detection project is a college team project. A small neural network scores every frame of an uploaded video as real or fake. A Streamlit web app shows a confidence chart and exports a PDF report. It reached 74.16% test accuracy on a random frame split. Co-built with Prasanna Patil and a classmate.
case_study.problem: Face-swap videos are hard to spot by eye, so reviewers need a quick, explainable first check. Without one, every clip needs careful manual review, and a fake that slips through can reach the news, a customer identity check or a hiring process. A bare yes or no also cannot be explained to a manager or a customer.
case_study.approach: The team trained the model on Celeb-DF, a public set of real and face-swapped videos. The first ten frames of each video are resized to 224 by 224 pixels and varied slightly with small shifts, zooms and flips. A small three-block neural network (a CNN, a model type for images) learns from the training split of 7,856 frames to give each frame a real-or-fake score. A six-page Streamlit app lets a reviewer upload a video. It scores every frame, averages the scores into a Real or Fake verdict, charts the score per frame and explains the score bands. A PDF report can be downloaded.
architecture: Data: Celeb-DF videos from the Celeb-real and YouTube-real folders are labelled real, those from Celeb-synthesis fake. The first ten frames of each video are resized to 224 by 224 pixels and split 80 to 20 at random, giving 7,856 training frames in the notebook's latest run.

Augmentation: training frames are varied slightly with rotation up to 10 degrees, small shifts, shear, zoom and horizontal flips. Test frames are only scaled to a 0 to 1 range, so the test is not changed by augmentation.

Model: a small three-block CNN. Three convolution layers of 32, 64 and 128 filters, each followed by pooling, then a dense layer of 64 units and a single 0 to 1 output (a sigmoid). It has about 5.6 million parameters and trains for 5 epochs with the Adam optimiser.

Verdict: each frame gets a score from 0 to 1. The app's confidence score is the mean of all frame scores as a percentage, and above 50 is Fake. It reads the bands as above 80 high confidence of a deepfake, 50 to 80 moderate, below 50 appears genuine.

App: a six-page Streamlit app with Home, Upload Video, Detection Results, How It Works, Feedback and About pages. It accepts mp4, mov, avi and mpeg files, previews the upload, scores every frame and draws a frame-by-frame chart of the scores.
Report: ReportLab builds a PDF with the video name, verdict, score, a reading guide for the bands and the first 40 frame scores.
Model delivery: the saved model file is fetched from Google Drive with gdown and cached by Streamlit, because the README treats a file over 25 MB as too big to upload.
results: 74.16% test accuracy on a random 20% share of frames held out from training, measured by the notebook's evaluate step. The team's own report lists this as room for improvement.
7,856 training frames of 224 by 224 pixels, from the first ten frames of each video in the Celeb-DF folders used. The saved model has about 5.6 million parameters, counted from the model file.
An end-to-end flow from upload to scoring, chart and PDF report in the app code, with screenshots of the upload, results and chart pages in the team's report.

h2.story: The problem: telling real video from fake
h2.arch: How each frame gets a verdict
h2.ext: What I can add for your videos

context: Newsrooms, banks that check identity on video, hiring teams and online platforms may receive video that has been altered. A face-swap clip can mislead an audience, pass a video identity check or damage a person's name. Reviewers who check every clip by eye cannot keep up, so they need a fast first filter that shows what to inspect.

A useful result is a first check, not a verdict. It scores a clip, shows which frames raised the score and produces a report a reviewer can file with the case. It also states how it was tested and where it fails, so that nobody mistakes a screening tool for proof.

challenges.title: Faint traces of a face swap
challenges.text: A good swap leaves only faint traces, such as small texture and colour mismatches around the face. A small model has to learn to spot them in single frames.

challenges.title: Near-identical frames
challenges.text: The first ten frames of a video look almost the same. A random split can put near copies in both training and test data, which can flatter the accuracy.

challenges.title: Limited computing resources
challenges.text: The team's report says limited computing resources restrict training depth. The model is small and trains for 5 epochs, and the app scores each frame of an upload one at a time.

challenges.title: Explaining the verdict
challenges.text: A reviewer needs more than the word "Fake". The app shows a score for every frame, a chart over the clip and a plain reading of the score bands, and the PDF keeps a record.

owned: Worked as one of three members of a college team that built the detector, the Streamlit app and the written project report.
Shared the work with Prasanna Patil and a classmate. The team's report does not record who did which part, so I claim no single module.
Published the repository from my account, with the training notebook, the app code and an early draft of the report. The final 31-page report is not in the repository.
context: The dataset, Celeb-DF, is a public research set of real and face-swapped videos. The model is a small CNN trained from scratch, not a pretrained network.
The README describes ResNeXt and LSTM models, and the How It Works picture adds face detection and cropping. The code has only the small CNN, and this page follows the code.

decisions.title: A small CNN on single frames
decisions.choice: The team trained a small three-block CNN on single frames, which its report records as a 3-layer ConvNet with augmentation and a sigmoid output.

decisions.title: Score every frame, then average

decisions.title: Plain bands for the score
decisions.choice: The app turns the average into three messages: above 80 high confidence of a deepfake, 50 to 80 moderate, below 50 appears genuine. The PDF repeats this guide.
decisions.why: A reviewer who is not a data scientist can act on a band. The cut-offs are fixed numbers, not calibrated probabilities, so they guide attention and prove nothing.

decisions.title: Celeb-DF and a random frame split
decisions.choice: Training used Celeb-DF, which the report calls a clean dataset, with a random 80 to 20 split of frames and a fixed seed so runs can be repeated.
decisions.why: One public dataset and a fixed seed keep the work repeatable. The trade-off is optimistic testing, because frames from one video can land on both sides, which a split by video would avoid.

limits: The 74.16% comes from a random split of frames, so frames of one video can sit in both training and test data. It likely flatters results on new videos, and the notebook gives no split of missed fakes and false alarms.

The model looks at whole frames, not cropped faces, and learned from the first ten frames of Celeb-DF videos only. The team's report says it is limited to videos like Celeb-DF and does not cover audio fakes.

The notebook's saved outputs come from different runs. The accuracy printout and the cell that shows 7,856 training frames were not run together, so treat them as the team's reported numbers, not one clean experiment.

The app saves each upload to a temporary file and does not remove it, and its score is an average of frame scores, not a calibrated probability. Treat the result as a first check for a reviewer, not as proof.

This project scores each frame as real or fake and combines the scores into a verdict. It is a first check for reviewers, not proof, because its accuracy is 74.16%.

faq.q: How can you detect a deepfake video?
faq.a: Use software as a first check and a person for the final call. This project resizes frames and scores each one with a small neural network. It averages the scores into Real or Fake and shows a confidence chart per frame. With 74.16% accuracy it points a reviewer where to look, and it cannot settle the question.

faq.q: How accurate is the detector?
faq.a: The notebook reports 74.16% on a random 20% share of Celeb-DF frames held out from training, so it is right about three times in four. Frames of one video can sit on both sides of the split, so results on new videos may be lower. The team's report lists it as room for improvement.

faq.q: Who worked on it?

faq.q: Does the detector find and crop faces first?
faq.a: No. The model sees the whole frame, resized to 224 by 224 pixels, with no face detection or cropping in the code. The README describes a ResNeXt and LSTM design (an image network plus a sequence model) and an app diagram shows face cropping, but the code builds neither. A face detector is an extension I can add.

faq.q: What data was the model trained on?
faq.a: Celeb-DF, a public deepfake dataset. Videos in its Celeb-real and YouTube-real folders are labelled real, and the Celeb-synthesis folder is labelled fake. The first ten frames of each video were resized to 224 by 224 pixels and split 80 to 20 at random, which gave 7,856 training frames. Training added small shifts, zooms and flips.

faq.q: Can I use this as proof that a video is fake?
faq.a: No. It is a first-check tool with 74.16% accuracy on one dataset, and its score is an average of frame scores, not a calibrated probability. The team's report says the tool is meant for education and not for public accusation. Use it to decide which clips a person should examine closely.

projects.title: Traceable AI Backend
projects.tagline: An AI server you can debug from the outside, with LLM observability built in.
projects.description_short: A FastAPI AI server where an AI picks the right business action for each question, with request IDs in logs, Prometheus metrics and OpenTelemetry traces in Jaeger for large language model (LLM) observability.
projects.role: Sole author. Design decisions and the options I rejected are logged in the repository.
projects.card_blurb: An AI server that shows exactly where each request goes and where it slows down, with request IDs, metrics and traces for LLM observability.

case_study.summary: This FastAPI OpenTelemetry tracing project is an AI server with LLM (large language model) observability built in. A request ID follows every call through logs, metrics and traces (viewed in Jaeger). This means a slow or failing call can be explained from the outside.
case_study.problem: An AI server can return a success code and still be slow, degraded or quietly answering from a different model. Nobody finds out until users complain. By then the cost is already paid: lost trust, a busy support queue and engineers searching logs with no way to tie a complaint to one request. Without counters, nobody can say how often it happens.
case_study.approach: I built a small AI server in FastAPI. For each question, an AI model picks one of three business actions, the action runs, and the model writes a short answer. Every log line and trace step of a request carries the same request ID, and the caller gets it back in the response. A few hand-written metrics count requests, AI response time, tokens (the small pieces of text an AI is billed by) and model fallbacks. Three Groq models are chained, each with its own time limit, and the response carries a "degraded" flag, so a silent fallback becomes visible. At work, I added resource use, service status and alerts to the LLM observability of the company's AI servers.
architecture: An AI server with an /ask endpoint (a web address the app answers on). An AI model picks one of three business actions: looking up tickets, creating a ticket or running a sales report. The action runs on made-up data, and the model then summarises the result.

A chain of three Groq models, each with a 10-second limit and the library's own retries switched off. If all fail, or no API key is set, a simple keyword router answers and the response is marked "degraded". The service therefore runs with no API key or internet.

One request ID, which is also the trace ID, appears on every JSON log line written during a request, on every trace step and in every /ask response, including errors. The question and the model's answer are deliberately kept out of the logs; only short error details are logged.

Hand-written Prometheus metrics: requests by status code, request time, errors by type, AI call time, tokens, model fallbacks and requests in progress. Labels are never free text, so the stored data stays small.

OpenTelemetry traces are pushed to Jaeger. The web request and the outgoing AI call are traced automatically, and I added spans for routing, the action, the summary and each model call. Health and metrics calls are left out.

A Docker Compose setup starts the app, Jaeger and Prometheus together. Configuration is baked into the images and every host port is a setting, so the stack can be copied to another machine and started the same way.
At the company, resource use, service status and alerts were added to the LLM observability of its AI servers. This part is confidential and is not part of the personal repository.
results: A deliberately slow lookup (a join over 60,000 made-up tickets) was the largest step in a trace. Once indexed, that step fell from about 15 seconds to under 50 milliseconds, and the whole request from about 16 seconds to under 1 second (captured traces).

10 automated tests that need no key or internet. They cover the health check, bad input, the unknown-region error, the metrics page, the AI path with a stand-in client, the model chain, the time limit and a provider failure.
A failing first model no longer hides. The fallback counter and the log line record it, and the trace shows a second attempt. When every model fails, the response is flagged "degraded".
A request that took about 12 seconds in testing was explained afterwards from the logs alone: the summary model hung, the 10-second limit fired and the second model answered in under half a second.
At the company, resource use, service status and alerts were added to the LLM observability of the AI servers. The details are confidential and are not published here.

h2.results: A slow step found in a trace

context: A business that puts an AI model behind a support tool, a report or a customer chat needs to know when that feature is slow, failing or quietly using a backup. If the team cannot see inside a request, every complaint turns into guessing: was it the model, the data or its own code? Visibility turns that guessing into a short search.

A good result lets anyone on the team take one complaint, find that exact request, see which step took the time and read the log lines for it. It also shows how heavily the AI servers are used, whether each service is running, and alerts people when something needs attention. This case study covers the request level and the server level, and says which part is which.

challenges.title: Failures that look like success
challenges.text: A missing or slow model can still end in a success code, because a backup path answers. That happened to me during testing, and my first logs and metrics gave no clear sign of it.

challenges.title: Finding the slow step
challenges.text: One request passes through a model call, a business action and a second model call. Total time alone does not say which step is slow. Only a step-by-step view does.

challenges.title: Telemetry that stays safe and small
challenges.text: Logs can leak customer text and grow fast. Metrics can multiply into thousands of series if a label holds free text. I kept questions and answers out of logs and used a short, fixed set of labels.

challenges.title: Seeing the servers, not only requests
challenges.text: A trace explains one call. It does not show whether the machine behind it is short of capacity or a service has stopped. That needs resource use, service status and alerts as well.

decisions.title: Tracing as the one big improvement
decisions.choice: Of seven options in the brief, I chose OpenTelemetry tracing, and I used the trace ID as the request ID on its log lines and responses.
decisions.why: Metrics show that a request was slow and logs show what the code did, but only a trace shows where the time went. One shared ID then links all three.

decisions.title: Hand-written logs and metrics
decisions.choice: I wrote a short log formatter and picked the metrics myself, instead of using ready-made helper libraries that choose them for you.
decisions.why: What to measure should be my decision and easy to explain. A helper library would have hidden the key idea, which is how the trace ID reaches each log line.

decisions.title: Fail fast, then try another model
decisions.choice: Each model gets a 10-second limit and the provider's own retries are off, so a failing model hands the request to the next one in the chain.
decisions.why: The provider's defaults could hold one hung model for up to 180 seconds. With my limit the worst case for one AI call is about 30 seconds across three models.

decisions.title: Leave out the large monitoring stack
decisions.choice: I declined Grafana, Loki, Tempo and Kubernetes, and used Jaeger and Prometheus on their own screens.
decisions.why: The task needed metrics, logs and traces that could be used, not a dashboard product. The extra tools would have added setup time and more containers without adding anything the task needed.

iteration.tried: I first set a single model, picked from the provider's public model list. On my key that model was not available, yet every request still returned a success code, because the keyword fallback quietly answered. The only sign was a flag in the response, and the log gave just an error class name.
iteration.changed: I replaced it with a chain of three models, ordered by the routing speed I measured (121, 492 and 545 milliseconds). I added the provider's error message to the log line and a fallback counter, so a failing first model shows up in monitoring even when users notice nothing.

limits: This is a job-application task, not a production system. The data is made up and held in memory, the slow lookup was planted on purpose, and the timings come from a single test setup, not real traffic.
Timings move with machine load: three repeat runs of the slow path took between 17.5 and 27.1 seconds. I report the captured pair as an example, not as an average.

The personal build records every trace, defines no alert rules and has no sign-in. A real service would sample traces, add alerts and secure access. The time limit covers AI calls only, not a slow business action.

faq.q: What is observability in a FastAPI app?
faq.a: Observability means you can tell what a running app is doing from the outside, using logs, metrics and traces. For an AI server this is called LLM observability. A request ID is stamped on every log line and trace step. Prometheus metrics count requests, AI response time and tokens. OpenTelemetry traces in Jaeger show where each request spent its time.

faq.q: Is this a production system?
faq.a: No. The traceable AI server is a job-application task, not a production system. The slow lookup was planted on purpose and the timings come from made-up data. The monitoring I added at work was for real company servers, but it is confidential and not shown here. A real system would need its own traffic, security and hosting decisions.

faq.q: Can it run without an AI key?
faq.a: Yes. With no key set, the server falls back to a simple keyword router and templated answers, and marks every response as degraded. Five of the 10 tests run in that mode. The others use a stand-in for the AI client or check its settings, so none needs a key, an account or internet.

faq.q: Which part is a personal build and which is company work?
faq.a: The traceable AI server is my own job-application build, written alone and kept in a private repository. The company work is separate: I added resource use, service status and alerts to the LLM observability of the company's AI servers. That work is confidential, so I describe it here but show none of its code, screens or figures.

faq.q: What happens if an AI model fails or hangs?
faq.a: A model that is unavailable, rate limited or silent for 10 seconds passes the request to the next of three Groq models. The fallback counter and the log line record each failure, and the response stays normal. If all three fail, simple keyword logic answers and the response is marked "degraded", so the caller knows no AI model wrote it.

faq.q: Do the logs store customer questions or answers?
faq.a: No. The question and the model's answer are deliberately kept out of the logs; only short error details are logged. Each line holds the request ID, the chosen action, row counts and durations. That protects privacy and keeps log volume down. Timing detail for one request lives in its trace.

faq.q: What does AI server monitoring add to request tracing?
faq.a: Tracing explains one request: which step ran and how long it took. Server monitoring watches what sits behind all requests. Resource use shows how much capacity the AI servers are using, service status shows whether each one is running, and alerts tell people when something needs attention. At work I added these to the company's LLM observability.

seo.title: WhatsApp AI Agent Case Study | Shaunak Chorge
seo.description: Case study: a WhatsApp AI agent backend built in an internship for a client. FastAPI, Redis and Celery send AI replies in the background.
seo.h1: WhatsApp AI agent that replies in the background

context: Many businesses talk to customers on WhatsApp: questions, bookings and updates. An AI agent can answer the routine messages, but only if it replies without making people wait, remembers who it is talking to and lets a human know when a person is needed. Without that, the chat turns into a slow, forgetful inbox.

A good result is a backend that receives each message, keeps a record of every user and conversation, and writes the AI reply in the background. Customers get automatic messages, staff get alerts, and the web layer stays free to take the next message. This project is that kind of backend, built for a client.
case_study.problem: A business that talks to customers on WhatsApp must receive every message, match it to the right customer and answer without making anyone wait. An AI model takes longer to reply than a web request should wait. If the reply is written inside that request, slow answers hold up the service. Without saved history, the agent forgets the customer, repeats questions and wastes staff time.

challenges.title: AI replies are slow
challenges.text: A language model takes longer to answer than a web request should wait, so the reply cannot be written inside the request that receives the message.

challenges.title: Remembering each customer
challenges.text: Every message arrives on its own. The platform must match it to the right user and bring back their state and history, so the conversation continues across sessions.

challenges.title: Reliable background work
challenges.text: Moving the AI work out of the request needs a queue and workers. Jobs must be handled reliably, so a reply can be written after the request has ended.

challenges.title: Two messaging providers
challenges.text: Customer messages and operator alerts rely on the Meta WhatsApp Business API and Twilio, so the platform has to work with both side by side.

case_study.approach: I built a backend (a message receiver, a job queue, background workers and a database) in Python with FastAPI. The receiver takes each WhatsApp message through a webhook, which is a web address that the messaging service calls, and tracks the user. The AI work goes onto a Redis and Celery job queue, and a worker writes the reply, so the AI never blocks the web request. PostgreSQL keeps user state and the full conversation history. The Meta WhatsApp Business API and Twilio carry customer messages and operator alerts.

decisions.why: A database lets the AI agent carry on a conversation across sessions and keeps interactions personal. Data held only in memory would be lost whenever the program restarted.

seo.title: SMS Spam Classifier Project | Shaunak Chorge
seo.description: SMS spam classifier project: TF-IDF and Naive Bayes on 5,169 text messages. 97.1% accuracy and no false alarms on 1,034 test messages.
seo.h1: SMS spam classifier project built with Naive Bayes

context: Teams that handle many incoming messages, such as a support desk or a shared inbox, lose time to spam, and scam messages put customers at risk. A trained text model can screen messages before a person reads them, so staff spend their time on the genuine ones. The harder part is doing that without hiding a message someone needs.

A good result is a filter that rarely blocks a genuine message, says how many spam messages it still misses, and can be retrained on a team's own labelled messages. This project is a small first version of that: a cleaned dataset, a measured model and a page where anyone can paste a message and see the label.
case_study.problem: Spam text messages waste time and carry scams. Checking each one by hand does not scale, and a filter that wrongly blocks a genuine message does more harm than one that misses a few spam messages, because the reader never sees what was blocked. The aim was to teach a small model to tell the two apart, and to measure how often it makes each kind of mistake.

challenges.title: Few spam examples
challenges.text: Only 653 of the 5,169 cleaned messages, about 13%, are spam. A model can look accurate by calling everything genuine, so accuracy alone says little.

challenges.title: Messy message text
challenges.text: Messages use abbreviations, numbers, symbols and odd spelling. The raw file also had 403 repeated messages and three mostly empty extra columns. All of it needed cleaning before any model could learn from it.

challenges.title: Blocking a real message
challenges.text: A false alarm hides a genuine message from its reader, which costs more than a missed spam. The model had to be judged on both kinds of mistake, not on one score.

challenges.title: Same cleaning in the page
challenges.text: The page must clean a pasted message exactly as the training messages were cleaned. Any difference would mean scoring words the model never saw, and the measured results would no longer apply.

case_study.approach: Following a public tutorial, I started from a labelled collection of 5,572 text messages and removed 403 repeats, which left 5,169. I cleaned each message with NLTK: lowercase, split into words, keep letters and digits, drop very common words and cut words to their roots. TF-IDF then scored the 3,000 most frequent words, and a Multinomial Naive Bayes model learned from a random 80% of the messages. I tested it on the other 20%, 1,034 messages, and saved the model and word scores to files. A Streamlit page and a command-line script load those files, repeat the same cleaning and show Spam or Not Spam.

flow.label: Clean text
flow.note: Lowercase, drop filler, cut to roots

architecture: A file of 5,572 labelled text messages. Three mostly empty extra columns were dropped and 403 repeated messages removed, leaving 5,169: 4,516 genuine and 653 spam.

Each message is made lowercase and split into words with NLTK (a Python toolkit for text). Punctuation and symbols are dropped, very common words (stop words) are removed, and words are cut to their roots with the Porter stemmer, so loving becomes love.
A TF-IDF vectoriser (scikit-learn) keeps the 3,000 most frequent words and scores each one by how often it appears in a message and how rare it is across all messages.

A Multinomial Naive Bayes classifier, a simple method that compares how often each word appears in spam and in genuine messages, with default settings. It learns from a random 80% of the messages (4,135); the other 20% (1,034) is kept for testing, split once with a fixed seed.
On the 1,034 test messages the confusion matrix shows all 896 genuine messages passed, 108 of 138 spam messages caught and 30 missed. That gives accuracy 97.10%, precision 100% and recall 78.26%.
The trained word scores and model are saved as two pickle files (Python's way of storing objects), each under 100 KB, so the page and the script load exactly what was tested.

A Streamlit page titled Email/SMS Spam Classifier, though only text messages were used, has a text box and a Predict button and shows Spam or Not Spam. A command-line script, predict.py, does the same for one message. Both repeat the cleaning steps first.

decisions.title: Remove repeats before splitting
decisions.choice: I removed 403 repeated messages before splitting the data, rather than leaving them in.
decisions.why: A message that appears in both the training and test sets would be recognised, not judged, and would lift the score. Removing repeats first keeps the test fairer.

decisions.title: Put precision first
decisions.choice: In the model comparison I ranked models by precision and kept one that blocked no genuine message, over several with higher accuracy.
decisions.why: A blocked genuine message is lost without its reader knowing, while a missed spam is only an annoyance. Precision and recall are reported next to accuracy because accuracy alone hides this.

decisions.title: Multinomial Naive Bayes over other models
decisions.choice: Following a public tutorial, I kept Multinomial Naive Bayes after a longer working notebook scored 14 other models and combinations on the same split, including Bernoulli Naive Bayes (98.4% accuracy, 1 false alarm).
decisions.why: Only it and nearest-neighbour search flagged no genuine message, and it was far more accurate than that one (97.1% against 90.5%). The saved model is also small, under 100 KB.

decisions.title: Save the model, reuse the cleaning
decisions.choice: I saved the trained word scores and model to files and repeated the exact cleaning steps in the page, rather than retraining or cleaning differently when the page starts.
decisions.why: The page always uses the exact objects that were tested, and a pasted message is cleaned like the training messages, so the measured scores still apply.

results: 97.10% accuracy on 1,034 test messages, a random 20% of the cleaned data, measured once in the notebook.
100% precision: none of the 896 genuine test messages was flagged as spam, so there were no false alarms.
78.26% recall: 108 of the 138 spam messages in the test set were caught and 30 were missed.
A filter that never flagged anything would still score 86.7% on this test set, because 896 of its 1,034 messages are genuine. That is why precision and recall are reported next to accuracy.
In the longer working notebook, 15 models and combinations were scored on the same split. Only two flagged no genuine message, and this one was the more accurate of the two.
The formal project report gives no accuracy number, so every figure on this page comes from the notebook output.
limits: Text messages only, in one language. No email was used for training or testing, so email accuracy is unknown. Emails are longer and carry subjects, links and attachments, so an email filter would need its own labelled data.

One dataset, one random split. The test result is a single measurement, and the word scores were learned from all messages before the split, so the figure is slightly optimistic. Newer scam wording would need fresh data.

It misses about one spam message in five (30 of 138 on the test set). A real filter would need a cut-off the owner can tune, a review folder for flagged messages and regular retraining on new messages.
It is a local demo: no automated tests, no monitoring, no link to any messaging system, and the requirements file pins older library versions than the ones that saved the model files.

use_cases.need: A team that reads many incoming messages could screen out likely spam first and send it to a review folder instead of deleting it, so genuine requests are not lost.
A company that sends and receives customer texts could flag scam or junk messages before staff or customers act on them, once the model is retrained on its own labelled messages.
A site with user messages or comments needs a first pass that flags promotions and scams for a person to confirm. A model retrained on the site's own labelled examples can supply it.
The project report names messaging apps and telecom services as places a filter could sit. A team there could use this build as a starting point and test it on its own traffic.

faq.q: How does a spam classifier for text messages work?
faq.a: A spam classifier turns a message into numbers and lets a trained model decide whether it looks like spam. Here the text is cleaned, each word is scored with TF-IDF, and a Naive Bayes model, trained on 4,135 of 5,169 labelled text messages, answers Spam or Not Spam.

faq.q: How accurate is this spam classifier?
faq.a: On 1,034 held-out text messages it scored 97.10% accuracy, 100% precision and 78.26% recall: no genuine message was flagged and 30 of 138 spam messages were missed. It is one random split of one dataset, so new messages, other languages or email could score differently.

faq.q: What do precision and recall mean for spam?
faq.a: Precision is the share of flagged messages that were truly spam. Recall is the share of all spam that was found. Here, on the test set, precision is 100%, so no genuine message was flagged, and recall is 78.26%, so about one spam message in five got through. A useful filter needs both numbers, not accuracy alone.

faq.q: Did you compare Naive Bayes with other models?
faq.a: The notebook in the public repository trains only Multinomial Naive Bayes. A longer working notebook, kept outside the repository, scored 15 models and combinations on the same split. Only two flagged no genuine message, and I kept Naive Bayes because it was the more accurate of those two.

faq.q: Can this spam classifier filter my company's email?
faq.a: Not as it stands. It learned from text messages only, so email was never tested. For email I would collect labelled examples of your own mail, retrain the model and measure precision and recall on messages it has not seen, before any message is blocked automatically.

faq.q: Is the spam classifier ready for production?
faq.a: No. It is an early-stage project built for an internship programme: one dataset, one test split and a local demo page. A production filter also needs fresh data, regular retraining, monitoring, a review queue for flagged messages and automated tests. I can build those around the model.

faq.a: I was the only author, with 20 commits. It was the project for the AICTE internship on AI delivered with TechSaksham, a Microsoft and SAP CSR initiative, under the programme's project guide. It follows a public tutorial, and it was submitted with a formal report that gives no accuracy figure.

items.q: Can I hire an AI engineer who also has a full-time job?
items.a: Yes. I am an AI Engineer at Claptek Pvt Ltd and take projects alongside the job. I am also open to full-time roles. For projects, we agree scope and timelines before work begins and you get regular progress updates. For roles, see my resume or write to me.

items.q: Can I hire you as a full-time AI Engineer?
items.a: Yes, I am open to the right full-time role. I currently work as an AI Engineer at Claptek Pvt Ltd in Mumbai. My resume, experience and project case studies are on this site. Send me a message and I will reply with my availability.

items.q: Do you take on freelance projects?
items.a: Yes. I take projects alongside my job. Send a short brief through the contact form or by email. I reply with questions and a first view of scope and timeline, and we agree the plan before work begins. I can take on work from small fixes to larger builds if the timeline fits.

items.q: What kinds of projects do you build?
items.a: I build AI chatbots that answer from your documents, tools that extract data from documents and Python backend APIs. I also build computer vision, speech and text models, and automation such as scrapers and Telegram or WhatsApp bots. Each area has its own page under Services.

items.q: What should I include in a project brief for an AI developer?
items.a: Say what you want to build and what a good result looks like, and roughly when you need it. Tell me anything I should know, such as private data, tools you already use or where it will run. Also say what you have already tried. A few lines are enough to start, and I ask for details later.

Send a short brief through the contact form or by email, as a few lines or a longer note. I read it, then reply with my view on feasibility and a proposed scope. We agree on both, and on a suitable deadline, before work begins.

items.q: Can you fix an existing AI project?
items.a: Yes. Most of my professional work has been inside software that already existed. I added an AI drafting service to a live audit product and sped up the core matching code during an internship. I read the code before changing it, keep changes tested and leave notes explaining each decision.

I work mostly in Python. For web services I use FastAPI and PostgreSQL, packaged with Docker (so it runs the same on any server). For AI I use services such as Groq and OpenAI, plus ChromaDB for document chatbots. For vision and speech I use OpenCV, PyTorch and TensorFlow. The full list is on the About page.

items.q: Can the AI run on our own servers instead of an online service?
items.a: Yes. At work I build on AI language models (LLMs) hosted on the client's own servers. This suits systems where no data, prompt or usage record may leave the building. My personal projects use online services such as Groq. We choose based on your privacy needs, cost and answer quality.

items.q: Can you sign a confidentiality agreement?
items.a: Yes. I am happy to sign a reasonable mutual NDA (a confidentiality agreement) before we discuss private details. I do not reuse client data or code in other projects. I only name a client or show their work in my portfolio with written approval.

items.q: Who owns the code you write for a project?
items.a: The ownership and licence terms are written into our agreement before work begins. The usual arrangement is that you own what you pay for. My freelance work is kept separate from my full-time job and never uses my employer's code or data.

items.q: What does a project look like from start to finish?
items.a: First we agree on the problem and how success will be measured. Then I build a small working prototype on your data. Next I add tests and safety checks. Finally I hand over notes and a walkthrough. You see working software early and get short written updates along the way.

items.q: What time zone does a Mumbai AI developer work in?
items.a: I am based in Mumbai, India, and work in Indian Standard Time (IST, UTC+5:30). I share written updates and code reviews, so you can always see where the work stands. We can agree meeting times that overlap with your working day. Earlier internships taught me how to keep distant teams in sync.

items.q: How much does it cost to hire an AI developer in India?
items.a: I do not publish a price list, because projects vary too much. After reading your brief, I suggest either a fixed price for a clearly defined scope, or hourly billing for open-ended work. The price and the terms are agreed in writing before I start.

items.q: How long does an AI project take?
items.a: It depends on the size of the project. After reading your brief, I give a written estimate for each step. A small prototype is much quicker than a full product. I give you a clear range, and we agree dates in writing before work begins.

items.q: What happens after you hand the project over?
items.a: Handover includes a README (a how-to guide), setup instructions, tests and a walkthrough, so your team can run and extend the work. A bug-fix period and ongoing maintenance can be agreed as part of the scope, and I will write down exactly what is covered.
